Rapid climate change brings wildfire threat to new corners of Europe

New Scientist September 03, 2026

Summer in Europe is no longer just a season of heatwaves and holidays. It is also, increasingly, a season of fire.

Following the pattern of recent years, 2026 saw huge fires break out across the continent, fuelled by weeks of hot, dry weather. Fires in France and Spain hit the headlines, but the UK, Belgium, Germany, Portugal and Italy have all also seen fierce blazes sweep through forests, grasslands and nature reserves.

Since the start of the year, almost 650,000 hectares of land have burned across the European Union, according to the European Commission, the result of over 1913 separate large wildfires across the bloc.

Advertisement

Canadian wildfires are reducing solar power generation in Europe

“Europe’s wildfires this summer have been extremely severe and destructive, and reached new corners of our continent,” Wopke Hoekstra, European commissioner for climate, net zero and clean growth, wrote on LinkedIn at the end of August. “The scale of what is happening is hard to ignore.”

On both sides of the Atlantic, the fire season has been far more severe than normal. In Europe, the area of land burned so far this year is almost double the long-term average. It is a similar story in the US, where the area of land burned so far this year is 163 per cent of the 10-year average.

But although this year has been bad by past standards, it still doesn’t come close to surpassing the devastation wildfires wreaked in 2025, still by far the most severe year on record for Europe, with more than 1 million hectares burned.

Instead, what has been notable about this year’s blazes is where they have appeared. Fires have burned across the European continent, but in southern Europe, traditionally the most fire-prone region, it has been relatively quiet. Northern and western European countries, however, like France, Belgium, the Netherlands and the UK – which aren’t used to dealing with severe wildfires – have suffered intense burns. For some, these have been larger and more widespread than what has been ever seen before.

Free newsletter

In England and Wales, for example, fire and rescue services have responded to 1132 wildfires so far this year, outstripping the total for the whole of 2025, which was itself a record year. The fires tore through homes, closed major roads, and crept perilously close to a nuclear power plant, all in a country better-known for its rain than its heat.

“I think what is particularly interesting for this season, in 2026, is not the total area burned… but how quicky conditions developed, and how geographically widespread the fire danger became,” says Francesca Di Giuseppe at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.

The conditions in Europe this year have been perfect for wildfires. An unusually wet winter encouraged rampant growth of grasslands, shrublands and forest understories. In May, the weather then shifted abruptly, bringing heatwaves in rapid succession and very little rainfall across swathes of the continent. The ground dried out, vegetation withered and a flash drought emerged on a grand scale. That left a dry, hot landscape littered with fuel. Add in high winds, and it was only a matter of time before fires broke out.

Will burying dead trees after a wildfire keep their carbon locked up?

“If you have 30 per cent of Europe fire-prone, somewhere it is going to happen,” says Di Giuseppe. “And if those conditions are sufficiently extreme, it will be very difficult to suppress the fire.”

This summer’s weather may have been unusually extreme, but it will become the new normal as global temperatures rise. Europe is one of the fastest-warming regions of the world. Across southern Europe, the number of summer days with fire-prone conditions has more than doubled since 1981, and the threat of catastrophic fires will only increase on the continent as the climate continues to warm, scientists predict. “The increasing frequency of hot, dry and windy conditions is consistent with the broader trend we expect under climate change,” says Maik Billing at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Research in Germany.

And, as we have seen this summer, in northern Europe the risk is rising rapidly from what was a low baseline. Managing the growing threat will require a significant shift in mindset, warns Alexander Held at the European Forest Institute. “When people outside of the UK think about the UK, they think of rain,” he says. “It you look at Ireland or Wales, where in a good year you have 2000 millimetres of rain, it is difficult for people to grasp that these landscapes are now burning.”

Why the extremes of climate breakdown will continue to take us by surprise

Much comes down to adopting common-sense behaviour in a fire-prone landscape – behaviour that is probably second nature to most citizens of southern Europe. In May, a major fire broke out at a Dutch military training ground, after the army trained with explosives during dry weather, prompting calls for training exercises to be halted at times of high fire risk.

In the UK, disposable barbecues were banned in August after they were found to have started fires in London, Staffordshire and Cheshire this summer. Simultaneously, the UK government sent out a nationwide alert to citizen smartphones, warning of a “very high risk of wildfires nationally” – the biggest use of the alert system to date – in the hope of curbing risky behaviours such as lighting barbecues or letting off fireworks.

Managing population movement from the countryside into cities is also a factor. In the US, urban sprawl has been blamed for bringing residents of cities such as Los Angeles into closer contact with the wildfire-prone countryside. But across Europe, rural abandonment is having the opposite effect; experts have warned that abandoned farmland provided plentiful fuel for the 2025 wildfires that swept through Greece, Turkey and Cyprus. The pruning, bush clearing and grazing that comes with managing a working farm is essential for fire suppression – policy-makers will need to find new ways to entice people back into the countryside to manage the fire frontiers.

The devastating wildfires in Europe demand urgent measures to make landscapes more resilient, but without action to reduce use of fossil fuels, the danger is only going to increase

Fire prevention can sometimes take the form of more unusual action – such as deer culling, says Held. In countries like the UK and Germany, earthworms are vital for clearing up leaf litter in forests before it becomes fire fuel in dry weather. But offering them the right species of leaf litter is important. In Germany’s Black Forest, for instance, earthworms love maple, cherry, lime and oak litter, but dislike conifer needles and beech litter. Unfortunately, the wild deer which roam the region’s woodlands have the same preference. As they graze and kill saplings, they are leaving the forests full of beech and conifers.

“You can see that in areas where we have too many deer, the decomposition of the [leaf] litter is not happening,” says Held.

In a similar vein, work is also needed to reshape forests to reduce monocultures and encourage native, broadleaf species which are more fire resistant. “It makes a big difference if you have a pine plantation with grass understory, where you have sunlight, wind, high temperature, drought, everything, or you have a very close to nature forest where you have shade, moisture, low temperature, no wind,” says Held.

Technology can also help. In May, a SpaceX rocket carried four new satellites into space, designed to help Greece better detect and track wildfires across its territories. FireSat is the same idea on a grander scale. Run by the non-profit Earth Fire Alliance with the help of Google, by 2030 it aims to have a constellation of 50 satellites scanning the most fire-prone spots on Earth, able to spot a fire as small as a beach bonfire. Three satellites entered orbit in July, joining the pilot satellite launched last year.

California bets on iron-salt battery power to protect against wildfire

Meanwhile, at ground level, feeds from camera networks can be monitored by AI software to spot the first signs of smoke. In California, a network of more than 1300 cameras covers fire-prone areas across the state. AI technology is used to scan the feeds and alert emergency services if fire is detected, with the aim of stopping fires before they have a chance to gather strength.

The system has helped firefighters react quickly to smother blazes that would have burned thousands of acres, according to Neal Driscoll at UC San Diego. The same technology is now arriving in Europe: in the Gironde, a region of France hit hardest by wildfires this summer, firefighters are now employing AI-assisted cameras to raise the alarm on emerging blazes. Solar-powered patrol drones could be next.

Yet fire management can take us only so far. Research published in August warns that by the end of this century, the area burned by wildfires in Europe will increase by 39 per cent even under a low-emissions scenario, and could almost triple under high emissions. Improvements in fire management could reduce these increases by more than 70 per cent, but not eliminate them entirely, the study found.

To reduce the growing risk of intense wildfires, California is cutting and burning the areas that fuel them – but these efforts may be moving too slowly

Some researchers think the fire risk is already beyond our control, particularly in southern Europe, which normally bears the brunt of “fire weather”. Raul Cordero Carrasco at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands points out that the burned area in southern Europe has been rising since 2018. He thinks this is a sign that investment in suppression and management is hitting its limit. In southern Europe, he argues, “climate change is making fires unstoppable”.

“When the temperature is very high and the winds are very strong, there is nothing you can do to stop the fire,” he says.

But for northern Europe at least, where large fires are still a mercifully rare event, there is plenty of work that can and must be done to mitigate further risk. Not every summer will be like the hot, dry days of 2026. But the threat is advancing, and this summer has been our amber warning to prepare.

Pygmy raccoons teach each other to make toys out of paper and sand

New Scientist September 03, 2026

Young pygmy raccoons on a Mexican island have been seen teaching each other to make toy balls out of rubbish, in a rare example of animals crafting objects purely for playing with.

“My first reaction was, oh my gosh, that’s absolutely adorable!” says Nessie O’Neil at Miami University in Ohio, who is researching the impact of tourism on the critically endangered pygmy raccoons (Procyon pygmaeus) of Cozumel Island.

Orcas have begun wearing salmon hats again – and we may soon know why

O’Neil filmed as one of the younger raccoons fished paper out of a rubbish bin, dipped it in a bowl of water and rolled it in sand, making a ball.

Advertisement

Over days of observation, she recorded the creatures as they made more balls and used them to play “football” with other raccoons and dwarf coatis (Nasua narica nelsoni), another raccoon-like animal. Siblings taught each other the ball-making procedure, and even tried to get their mother involved, though she couldn’t quite figure it out – her coordination seemed to have been impaired after drinking a margarita she found at a beach bar earlier that day.

O’Neil’s colleague at Miami University, Michelle Szydlowski, was impressed by the footage. While others have watched animals like chimps or tigers at play, researchers have seldom seen animals custom-making toys for later use. “It shouldn’t be surprising that raccoons are where we’re seeing this, just because they’re so tactile, they see with their hands,” says Szydlowski.

Free newsletter

“The observations show how complex animal play behaviour can be,” says Marek Špinka at the Institute of Animal Science in the Czech Republic. “It will be intriguing to see whether the behaviour will get a hold in the population as a new cultural trait or will disappear.”

The observations may also help with conservation efforts. There are fewer than 200 pygmy raccoons on Cozumel, the only place the species is found. Understanding how they learn from each other might help conservationists discourage unhealthy behaviours like stealing margaritas and begging for snacks, and reacquaint them with foraging in the wild. And O’Neil hopes increased awareness of the animals will bring more support. “I really just want people to know that they are out there, and they need people to care,” she says. “And please don’t feed them!”

‘Not-quite primordial’ black holes may explain baffling JWST discovery

New Scientist September 03, 2026

There may have been black holes in the early universe before the first stars, and a group of theoretical physicists has proposed a new way to explain how they could have formed using the heat of the cosmic microwave background. The idea may be a better explanation for the “little red dots” identified by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) – distant galaxies that seem to host surprisingly large numbers of astonishingly ancient black holes.

“James Webb is discovering many more black holes than most of us theorists predicted in our most optimistic models,” says Priyamvada Natarajan at Yale University. “The universe is just littered with black holes.”

An existing idea is that primordial black holes formed in violent space-time spasms in the early universe before any stars appeared. But these violent spasms are hard to reconcile with the milder ripples that astronomers see in the cosmic microwave background (CMB), faint light left over from the primordial universe. Theorists have had to propose complicated new physical laws to make the explanation fit.

Advertisement

We may have found a surprisingly nearby cluster of primordial stars

Wenzer Qin and Neal Weiner at New York University and Soubhik Kumar at Tufts University in Massachusetts realised there was another option. They began by assuming milder ripples of dark matter moved through the early universe, and argued that large black holes would be able to form inside clumps of this dark matter, with the hot CMB keeping gas and dust from collapsing into smaller ones instead.

They call these black holes “not-quite-primordial” and argue they provide an explanation for the black holes spotted via the JWST that doesn’t require drastic changes to cosmologists’ picture of the early universe.

The researchers reached out to Natarajan, a theoretical astrophysicist, to help confirm their logic.

“This is a case where you could actually have a black hole forming before the stars. And that I found really exciting,” says Natarajan.

Subscriber-only newsletter

“What’s nice about the model is that it invokes less speculative physics than traditional primordial black hole physics,” says John Regan at Maynooth University, Ireland, who wasn’t involved in the paper. “Having says that, what we need ultimately will be concrete observations. We’ll need to see some ultra-early-Universe signatures of black holes, be that from gravitational waves or from some future CMB observations, to see if black holes truly existed at the very earliest times.”

Qin and collaborators are getting ready for those observations. Their next step will be to simulate the new process and see what it implies about the spectrum of light that should be emitted from around a not-quite-primordial black hole. They can then compare these predictions more closely to data from JWST.

They are also looking forward to future satellite telescopes like the proposed Primordial Inflation Explorer (PIXIE), which should be able to measure the CMB spectrum well enough to find evidence for their proposal.

Physical Review Letters DOI: 10.1103/zfjm-8fnt

More than 3000 lightning strikes have been recorded in the past 12 hours and 135km/h gusts have hit Wellington as wild weather moves up the country.

Heavy rain has also hit places like Mt Cook Village, with more than 90mm falling in 12 hours as the front moves over Fiordland and Southland, MetService meteorologist Heather Keats told Ryan Bridge TODAY.

Gales, heavy rain, thunderstorms, hail and even a touch of snow have all been forecast for some areas before a second system drags wet weather across most of the country on Sunday.

Some flights in and out of the capital have been affected, with multiple cancellations showing for Wellington Airports arrivals and departures. Some flights have managed to make it through, however, including some on smaller, regional aircrafts.

Keats said high winds with gusts over 210km/h had been measured in the Canterbury high country, while Wellington’s Mt Kaukau weather station had registered a 135km/h gusts.

A second round of watches and warnings was expected for the weekend, as a new low forming in the Tasman Sea was likely to make conditions “pretty miserable” as it raced over the country.

Sunny skies and mild temperatures are still possible for northern New Zealand, including Auckland and the Bay of Plenty, but heavy rain is possible late on Sunday or early on Monday morning – with potential issues for commuters.

The timing of this weekend’s weather was still “iffy”, Keats said, but lots of thunderstorms were likely, along with potential hail, for the entire west coast up to Taranaki, as well as Southland up to Dunedin.

“There is also the chance of small tornadoes with those for the west coast too,” Keats said.

A handful of watches and warnings have been issued, with strong northwesterly winds expected to affect eastern parts of the South Island and the lower North Island today.

An orange strong wind warning is in place for Wellington and Wairarapa (excluding the Tararua District) this morning, with severe gale northwesterlies gusting 130km/h in exposed places.

Strong wind watches have also been issued for Marlborough this morning, and Hawke’s Bay and the Tararua District between 9am and 4pm tomorrow.

A nine-hour strong wind watch begins at midnight tonight for Canterbury’s high country and on the plains close to the foothills.

The front that brought heavy rain to parts of the South Island last night was moving north and was expected to reach central New Zealand around midday, MetService forecaster Sophie Huntington said.

An orange heavy rain warning was in place for the headwaters of the Canterbury lakes and rivers about and south of Arthur’s Pass National Park from midnight until 8am, with up to 130mm in the area of the main divide and lesser amounts to the east.

A nine-hour heavy rain watch for the ranges of Buller began at midnight, and wild conditions could be a feature for some in the South Island.

“Thunderstorms are possible as the front moves up the South Island, bringing strong wind gusts and hail. The front then weakens as it pushes up the North Island.”

Rain was also expected to turn to snow showers from this morning on Milford Rd (State Highway 94), with up to 8cm possible at the Homer Tunnel and lesser amounts to 600m.

Despite the unsettled weather in the west, eastern parts of the country could expect mild temperatures and sunny spells, Huntington said.

“However, increasing high cloud, particularly across the South Island, may take the edge off the sunshine at times.”

Highs of around 18C are forecast in Auckland over the next three days, although afternoon showers tomorrow could be briefly heavy, with a similar outlook for Whangārei, Hamilton and Tauranga.

A high of 23C is forecast in Hastings tomorrow – with 22C in neighbouring Napier – with mostly fine weather through the weekend, bar a few showers this afternoon and Sunday evening.

In Christchurch, highs in the late teens are forecast for the next three days, but that will be tempered by rain on Sunday.

That wet turn is caused by a low-pressure system developing in the Tasman Sea, expected to bring widespread rain and showers to end the weekend, Huntington said.

“The South Island is likely to see the heaviest falls, with rain not reaching parts of the North Island until late.”

For those heading to the Aims Games in Tauranga, a fine start to the event was expected, with some showers possible on Monday, she said.

Nearly 30,000 people are expected in the city before the annual sporting event for intermediate-aged children.

A wind change would likely temper the warmer temperatures enjoyed by many late this week, Huntington said.

“Next week looks like a shift towards more southwesterly winds, so temperatures will come down a notch.”

Hopscotch Beer Company: Covid fallout forces founder to sell West Auckland microbrewery after 15 years

New Zealand Herald September 03, 2026

Hopscotch Beer Company founder Hugh Grierson says a "discriminatory" rule sent his company into a "death spiral". Photos / NZME, Supplied

A West Auckland business owner says the unequal treatment of liquor retailers during Covid caused lasting damage, ultimately forcing him to sell his company and life’s work.

Hopscotch Beer Company founder Hugh Grierson has sold his Avondale store after 15 years, saying the business never recovered from lockdown rules that only allowed trust-owned liquor stores to open while independent retailers such as his remained closed – something he says is an example of “small businesses getting shafted”.

However, the Chief Ombudsman did not uphold Grierson’s complaint about the Government’s decision, concluding the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) had not acted unreasonably.

Grierson told the Herald his Wolverton St business, a small brewery that sold craft beer for take-home customers, had gone down a “death spiral” since Covid.

While liquor stores weren’t able to open for the vast majority of the country during Covid lockdowns, they were allowed to operate in areas such as West Auckland and Invercargill where alcohol is controlled by licensing trusts, a post-prohibition system where beer and wine can’t be bought at supermarkets.

After independent retailers were allowed to trade during the first nationwide Level 4 lockdown, Cabinet instructed MBIE officials to restrict liquor-shop operations in monopoly areas to outlets run by licensing trusts, preventing Hopscotch and other independent alcohol retailers from opening.

Contact the Herald newsroom

Grierson called the policy “discriminatory” as it was based on ownership and allowed his competitors to operate while small businesses like his were told to shut.

“It’s a bad situation for your business when you’re shut and your opposition is open,” Grierson said.

“If I got to trade and got the same treatment The Trusts did, I’d say I’d definitely still be there.”

The Trusts chief executive Allan Pollard told the Herald the events happened before his time and he was unable to comment on Grierson’s case, but added: “I welcome any competition into the market.”

Grierson said his protestations and complaints about what he and many others described as unfair fell on deaf ears, with his business forced to stay shut throughout Auckland’s multiple lockdowns.

“I was trying to get to trade again because I didn’t want to be taking government money.”

Grierson said his business’ situation worsened after Inland Revenue audited him and found he owed about $30,000 in Covid support repayments, which he said ballooned to $64,000 with interest and penalties.

Grierson said Inland Revenue required him to repay some of the support because he had continued paying himself while also being a shareholder in the company.

He said he had believed the payments were permitted because they were wages for his work as the business’s sole employee, rather than dividends.

“I kept giving myself exactly the same amount of money [prior to Covid] because I was still working and still eating and trying to feed my kids.

“Just like most small businesses in New Zealand I’d say if they got audited most of them would have broken those rules because they weren’t making money and they needed to live.”

Grierson believes the barriers that worked against him are examples of small businesses “getting shafted” and “swept under the rug”.

“How many businesses have been wound up because of debts from Covid?

“Pre-Covid, business was growing and I was planning on diversifying a bit more of a range, being a bit less of just a craft beer shop … but that all kind of fell over.

“And now my stock levels are down, and if I get a GST refund, Inland Revenue takes it. If you make money, Inland Revenue wants it. So I just have to get out.”

Inland Revenue told the Herald Section 18 of the Tax Administration Act prevented it from commenting on an individual taxpayer’s affairs.

Chief Ombudsman Peter Boshier did not uphold Grierson’s official complaint about the unfairness of the liquor retailer rule change, concluding MBIE “has not acted unreasonably”.

Boshier noted in his final opinion into the complaint that he was satisfied the decision was made by Cabinet, despite the absence of minutes or other records documenting it.

“I have already expressed to the ministry my concerns around its record-keeping,” Boshier said in June 2022.

“I noted that it is fundamentally important that records of significant decisions like this are created and maintained – noting the significant effect of this decision on people like Hugh.”

When approached by the Herald, an MBIE spokesperson said: “The ombudsman thoroughly investigated this and confirmed in his response that Cabinet made this decision not MBIE.

“Cabinet provided oral instruction to MBIE officials to restrict bottle stores opening during lockdown to those that were operated by liquor licensing trusts in monopoly areas. This was to enable reasonable access to purchase retail alcohol locally.”

Grierson managed to find a buyer and sold his business last month, including its name, brand and brewing operation to preserve its liquor licence, which allowed him to settle most of his debts.

But it still hasn’t made up for the thousands in start-up capital and “all my life and all the work”.

After years of fighting the Covid-era decision and attempts to keep his business alive, Grierson said he’s looking forward to putting it all behind him.

He is now a fulltime science teacher and will continue to brew as a hobby.

“I’m sleeping better,” he said. “I pity all the poor small businesses who are still getting ruined.”

Union members on the Interislander ferries have given notice of partial industrial action after reaching an “impasse” over controversial new laws relating to personal grievances.

The action will not be a stoppage of the Cook Strait ferries, but rather affected members will refuse to load KiwiRail cargo units or work callbacks or any overtime on September 18.

KiwiRail’s chief operations officer Duncan Roy said they had received the notice of industrial action and were assessing potential impacts on operations.

The dispute relates to a bargaining claim for KiwiRail to agree to the Government’s “opt back in” personal grievance provisions, which were introduced as part of a law change affecting personal grievance access for employees above a certain income threshold.

Under the new legislation, people who earn more than $200,000 per year are unable to pursue an unjustified dismissal claim against their employer, unless they had opted out of this clause by contract.

The legislation says these earners were “likely to have high bargaining power” and the changes would provide greater “flexibility and certainty in the dismissal process for employees who have a significant impact on organisation performance”.

The law comes into effect in February 2027 for existing employees, and would remove protections allowing them to challenge an unjustified dismissal and seek reinstatement.

“The law was aimed at quicker removal of non-performing middle and upper management, including CEOs, but has captured many other employees, such as airline pilots, medical specialists, ships’ masters and senior officers, maritime pilots and can extend to other employees who, with overtime, reach the income thresholds, such as Kiwirail’s senior train drivers,” said unions NZ Merchant Service Guild (MSG) and Aviation and Marine Engineers Association (AMEA) in a joint statement.

The unions raised the issue as part of the bargaining for the renewal of the collective agreement.

“The company’s refusal has come as a surprise to the unions and their members,” the unions said.

“KiwiRail otherwise maintains constructive working relationships with the unions representing its employees.”

The unions said the claim posed no cost to KiwiRail, but sought to “maintain the status quo” for employee protections around dismissals.

They said there were 233 employees who met the income threshold, and that KiwiRail had advised they would not continue protections for any of those people.

“Only a very small number of those KiwiRail employees impacted by the law change are employed on the ships.”

For the MSG, those were the members in senior roles only – masters and chief officers, and a fraction of KiwiRail’s total workforce of 4500.

The masters, officers and engineers are responsible for the safe passage of the ferries in a “hostile and unpredictable body of water”, which the unions described as “one of the most dangerous stretches of water in the world, with frequent wild weather and sea conditions”.

“A large portion of the crossing involves navigation in close quarters with little margin for error.”

Should an accident occur, those officers were ultimately held responsible, and a master was subject to civil and criminal liability with penalties including possible prison time, the unions said.

“The union and its members see unjustifiable dismissal and reinstatement protections as a crucial check on employers in safety-critical industries, which prevents them from exerting commercial pressure on employees to override their legal duties to put safety first at all times.”

Bargaining began in February and the parties have met several times since May to progress it.

“The Interislander employees are not asking for large pay increases this year, but just want the company to support its workforce and not to threaten their job security,” said the unions.

The industrial action would not affect passengers or non-KiwiRail cargo, or private and commercial vehicles. Bluebridge ferries are not affected.

The unions said they were open to mediation, saying a settlement was achievable “provided the employer demonstrates it values its employees and agrees to follow the new law’s inbuilt mechanism for maintaining existing personal grievance rights for them”.

Roy said the company’s focused remained on continuing negotiations and minimising disruption for customers wherever possible.

“We have no further comment at this stage.”

Melissa Nightingale is a Wellington-based reporter who covers crime, justice, and news in the capital. She joined the Herald in 2016 and has worked as a journalist for 12 years.

Mount Maunganui landslide: Tauranga City Council has conflict of interest as campground owner – Academic

New Zealand Herald September 03, 2026

Tauranga City Council’s dual role as campground owner and regulator created a conflict of interest in managing risk, a local government expert believes.

The council says it has a policy for managing conflicts of interest and systems for regulating its assets ethically.

Six holidaymakers died when a landslide from Mauao crashed into the council-owned Mount Maunganui Beachside Holiday Park about 9.30am on January 22 after record rainfall.

Tauranga City Council’s external review into the fatal landslide, led by former High Court judge Paul Davison, KC, found the tragedy was “preventable”.

Davison identified reports of landslide risk and rockfall hazards for the campground going back to 1999.

A 2025 geotechnical report warning of risk to life for campground visitors was sent in an agenda to multiple councillors who did not read it, after the meeting was cancelled.

The Bay of Plenty Times requested but has not yet received details of the council’s income from the holiday park.

The council elected to consider the request under official information legislation, which allows 20 working days for a response.

The council’s 2020/21 annual report said the campground generated just under $2.2 million that year, the first time revenue exceeded $2m.

The report also said 85,452 guests stayed at the campground in that period.

The Bay of Plenty Times asked Dr Andy Asquith from the University of Western Australia for his views on the council’s role as regulator for its commercial asset.

The local government expert and former Massey University academic said, in his opinion, it was impossible for a regulator to act independently with its own assets.

He said, speaking generally, he had never seen a council successfully manage both commercial activities and their regulation.

He said the idea of self-regulation was “oxymoronic”.

“You can’t police yourself. When you have a conflict of interest, you can’t [look at risk and risk mitigation] in a transparent, fair way.”

Council regulatory and community services general manager Sarah Omundsen said the council managed regulation through policies and external oversight.

She said the council administered regulation for a range of assets it owned and operated.

Omundsen said the council had a policy for monitoring its compliance with the legislation it enforced, as it did for other regulated parties.

She said the council had a framework for enforcement decisions, which were considered by an enforcement decision group and legal adviser.

“The policy commits [the] council to lawful, ethical and impartial decision-making and to transparency of decision-making.”

Omundsen said the council had a separate conflicts of interest policy.

“Where [the] council is the applicant for a regulatory approval, the conflict is clearly identified, rigorously assessed, and transparently managed to protect regulatory integrity and public trust.”

She said building services staff managed conflict for council-owned property and any commercial, financial or other pressures that could affect independence.

Bay of Plenty Regional councillor Stuart Crosby, who was Tauranga Mayor from 2004 to 2016 and is a former president of Local Government NZ, said it was common for councils to operate a commercial activity.

Crosby previously told the Bay of Plenty Times he did not recall any landslide reports reaching his desk – as did several other former mayors and leaders.

He said council-owned entities must comply with council and Government regulations.

“They don’t get a free pass on that in any way, shape or form.”

The Bay of Plenty Times asked Crosby if the council’s commercial interests in the campground when he was mayor influenced its response to landslide risk.

Crosby said he saw no evidence of that.

He said the issue was the flow of information.

“Where there is that conflict of interest, those issues should be handled independently by independent people outside of council.”

A Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport spokesperson said councils had responsibilities for identifying, assessing, communicating and managing known natural hazard risks.

They said councils were required to manage natural hazard risks under the current Resource Management Act 1991.

District councils were required to have hazard provision plans and regulate development in hazard-prone areas through zoning and consent rules, they said.

The spokesperson said councils also led local response and recovery efforts during natural disasters through the Civil Defence Emergency Management (CDEM) structure.

“[A council] must identify and assess hazards and risks within its district or region, manage these risks, report those risks to the CDEM group, and communicate about those risks with any affected communities.”

The spokesperson said a council owning and operating a business would be a “person conducting a business or undertaking” under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015.

It had a duty to ensure the health and safety of workers and the public.

“It [the person conducting a business or undertaking] must also meet responsibilities set out in legislation, such as under the Local Government Act and the Resource Management Act.”

The spokesperson said local authorities should conduct business openly and transparently.

Commercial transactions must be in accordance with sound business practices, they said.

Bijou Johnson is a multimedia journalist based in Bay of Plenty. A passionate writer and reader, she grew up in Tauranga and developed a love for journalism while exploring various disciplines at university. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in Classical Studies from Massey University.

Stokes Valley fatal fire trial: Henare Barber says texts referred to drug house, not arson

New Zealand Herald September 03, 2026

Arden Neho (from left), Henare Barber and Reardon Kamaru are on trial in the High Court at Wellington for the murder of Ian Moller (inset).

A gang member accused of directing others to burn down a block of flats insists text messages between them referred to a drug house, not arson.

Henare Barber has taken the stand in his defence at his murder trial in Wellington, where he and fellow Mangu Kaha gang members Arden Neho and Reardon Kamaru deny charges of murder and arson after a fire at a block of Kāinga Ora flats in November 2024.

There were three fires at the flats in Stokes Valley in October and November 2024, with the final incident in the early hours of November 5 proving fatal.

Neho also denies two charges of arson relating to the two earlier fires. A fourth man, Shyheim Aiga, has pleaded guilty to charges arising from the two earlier fires and will be dealt with separately.

On the night of the last fire, pensioner Ian Moller was carried by firefighters from his upstairs flat, where he’d lived for 23 years, and rushed to hospital. He died five days later.

The Crown’s case is the fires were carried out under the direction of the gang and specifically Barber, a patched Mangu Kaha member. In return, it said, Neho, Kamaru and Aiga received their patches.

Under questioning from his lawyer Shane Robinson, Barber repeatedly denied instructing or directing anyone to light the fires, saying he wouldn’t do that and telling the jury he had no criminal convictions.

“I would never jeopardise my life that I have with my family to try to hurt someone else. I want to be there for my kids,” he told the court.

He didn’t know Moller, other than by sight, and had no reason to harm him, he told the jury.

Central to the Crown’s case is a volume of text messages between the defendants and others in the days and weeks leading up to the fires.

“The Crown says the messages in these books are about you directing or encouraging your co-defendants to commit arson,” Robinson put to his client.

“No,” Barber responded.

Instead, he explained the messages were about drug dealing, with references to “missions” or a “mess” referring to a house in Stokes Valley where he knew drugs were being sold.

“I just wanna smash that mission tonight f*** I just wanna get it done and patch use up tomorrow,” Barber texted one of the prospects.

Because it was a Mangu Kaha area, the gang would send people to the address and give them an ultimatum: either pay a $500 weekly fee to keep selling drugs or sell drugs on the gang’s behalf.

In exchange, those in the household would be offered protection from other gangs.

The three weren’t long from being patched and he saw an opportunity for a house in the valley where drugs were being sold, he said.

“It was an opportunity to get a good resume.”

Asked by Robinson why he hadn’t told police when interviewed, Barber said he didn’t want police to bust it.

But under cross-examination by Crown prosecutor Anselm Williams, Barber admitted that in November 2024 he wasn’t running any drug houses.

He said three drug houses had been under gang control before 2024, but they ceased with the death of another gang member in 2023.

Since then, there had been no gang involvement.

“So you took it upon yourself to set up this arrangement?” Williams asked.

“Yep,” Barber responded.

He accepted that for the three to get their patches, they had to complete their mission, but repeatedly told the court that mission involved a drug house, not arson.

He wasn’t sure if the mission was completed because he was dealing with two family bereavements around that time, including the death of his father.

He also didn’t attend their patching ceremony at Taitā Cemetery, held the same day as Moller’s death.

He insisted he wasn’t a ranked member of the gang and had no sway over who was patched.

He told Williams he was never asked to do things for the gang, nor was he responsible for ensuring the prospects did their jobs, but he agreed he could ask a prospect to do something for him, although he told the court he never did.

Contact the Open Justice team

Earlier, Kamaru gave evidence in his defence.

Questioned by Williams about a text from an associate to Kamaru, which said, “Go burn more houses down ... and get innocent people killed like last time”, he denied this implied his guilt, telling the jury the associate was lying.

He agreed he’d asked an associate to delete messages off their phone, telling the jury he was worried about mention of drug dealing, only to concede the two didn’t exchange any messages about drug dealing.

“It just makes me feel better,” he said.

When it was put to him that texts and messages from others also suggested he was responsible for the fatal fire, he denied this was the case.

“Were you involved in starting the fire on November 5?” Williams asked.

“No,” Kamaru responded.

“That’s just another one of your lies,” Williams said.

“No,” Kamaru responded.

The Crown will make its closing address on Friday, with the defence expected to give theirs next week before Justice David Boldt sums up the case for the jury.

Catherine Hutton is an Open Justice reporter, based in Wellington. She has worked as a journalist at the Waikato Times and RNZ. Most recently she was working as a media adviser at the Ministry of Justice.

New Zealand Herald September 03, 2026

A New Zealand farmer and adventurer competing on Alone Australia has revealed for the first time the tragic accident that fatally injured his father, saying he has never spoken about it with anyone, not even his wife.

Clint Waghorn, a 57-year-old off-grid sheep and beef farmer, spoke about his father after surviving 37 days alone in the remote wilderness of Sapmi, Finland, where he is competing against nine Australians in Season 4 of the hit survival series.

As hunger, exhaustion and isolation mounted, Waghorn reflected on a day nearly 31 years ago that changed his life forever.

“It’s been nearly 31 years since he passed away. I’ve never talked about it with anyone. Not even my wife,” he said.

“I’m not even sure if I can, to be honest.”

Waghorn told the camera he had spent a spring day helping a neighbouring farmer while his father remained at home carrying out jobs around the family farm.

Returning later that afternoon in a farm ute, he came around a corner to find his father approaching from the opposite direction on a four-wheeler.

“He didn’t see me. He hit the front of the ute. It was enough for him to fly over the handlebars.”

The bike plunged down a bank while his father was left badly injured beside the driveway.

“I went and got help, called the ambulance. By the time they got there, he was deteriorating. We knew there was something badly wrong.”

An air ambulance was called, but his father died on the way to hospital.

The loss was devastating for Waghorn, who described his father as a parent and a mate.

“Dad and I were bloody close. We hunted together, we fished together, worked together, drank beer together, watched sport on TV together.

“To lose your dad and your mate in one blow like that, bloody hell.”

The revelation marked a rare display of vulnerability from the self-reliant farmer, who has built a life around resilience and endurance.

Living off-grid on a remote sheep and beef farm, Waghorn powers his property with solar energy and raises much of his own food. His outdoor credentials include a 10,000km sea-kayaking expedition around Alaska, which became the subject of a book, and a 14-day solo survival challenge in the New Zealand wilderness.

But despite a lifetime spent tackling physical hardship, Waghorn said the memory of his father’s death remained difficult to confront.

He said the tragedy shaped his outlook on life.

“If there’s one thing I took from that fateful day all those years ago, it’s make the best use of what time I’ve got every day.”

The reflection came as Waghorn continued battling dwindling food supplies more than a month into the competition.

“You can fish all day, be nothing, nothing, nothing. Then suddenly you get one bite and it just can make everything worthwhile.”

University of Auckland student caught wearing smart glasses in exam

New Zealand Herald September 03, 2026

A University of Auckland student has been caught wearing smart glasses in a test. Photo / Getty Images

By Luka Forman of RNZ

A University of Auckland student has been caught wearing smart glasses in a test, raising concerns about how the new tech could be used by students to cheat.

New products like Meta glasses have small built-in cameras which can be used to film what is in front of them, and have it answered by an outside helper or AI.

Exam supervisors would now have to check students wearing glasses to their exams to see if they could be using them to cheat.

Gone are the days of trying to smuggle pieces of paper into an exam or writing answers on a hand or water bottle label.

Technology has brought new ways for students to try to cheat their tests, as computer science professor at the University of Auckland Ulrich Speidel explained.

“You can go, for example, and record your questions, you can possibly send them to external helpers and most of those glasses also project stuff into the glasses that only the wearer can see.”

A University of Auckland spokesperson said a student was seen wearing smart glasses during a test by an invigilator, after a pre-test announcement explicitly said no smart glasses or watches were allowed.

The student had the glasses taken off them, and was allowed to continue the test, they said.

The student was given a penalty over the incident, but the university would not say what it was.

Ulrich Speidel said exam invigilators would now be on the lookout for smart glasses.

“Generally what you can see is they’ve got rather broad hinge parts or large bridges, so we can ask our invigilators to go and look for those, and for example ask [or] offer masking tape to be put over them.”

Invigilators would tape over the cameras rather than taking the glasses, if students were using them as prescriptions.

Meta, the company that owned Instagram and Facebook, had two models of smart glasses made with brands Rayban and Oakley.

They retailed for between $350 and $750, depending on the model.

On the cheaper end, Kmart sold its own smart glasses for just $99 – which recorded videos and photos but did not have the AI features of the Meta ones.

Engineering student at AUT, Preston Williams, had a pair of the Meta glasses, which he used to make content for his business.

“I’ve got like a detailing business, so I do like POV [point of view] videos and stuff. But I don’t use it for tests, because there’s a massive white flashing light. So it’s kind of hard to be inconspicuous.”

However, that flashing light could be disabled through a relatively quick repair job.

US tech journalist Joanna Stern found in an investigation that dozens of services were available to do just that for about US$100 on Facebook Marketplace.

However, those services did not appear to be available online in New Zealand.

Speidel said the university was keeping on top of cheating in exams, for now.

“I dread the day once smart glasses will be available as contact lenses. At that point I think it will be checkmate for us.”

His department has moved to mostly pen and paper tests with randomised multi-choice questions, meaning each student had different tests to their peers.

The University of Auckland spokesperson said it undertook an academic integrity investigation into the student with the smart glasses, resulting in a penalty for the student.

The critics have spoken: Add these books to the stack

Sydney Morning Herald September 04, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

There are some big forces at work in this week’s new releases: oceans, technology, history, motherhood and the occasional supernatural presence. Our five novels range from a Hawaiian love story shaped by disaster to a wonderfully strange satire in which childbirth produces a rather alarming new mother. In non-fiction, Thomas Mayo considers fathers and sons, George Megalogenis takes Australia’s temperature, and Toby Walsh contemplates a future dominated by AI.

Everything to the Sea by Alicia Upano (Bloomsbury, $35)Hawaiian writer Alicia Upano delivers an impressively restrained love story from amid the epic ruin caused by a tsunami. Growing up in Hilo, Hawaii, Jane is an architecture student whose ambitions call her away to university. Summer holidays draw her back to Hilo, where she falls unexpectedly in love with Kenji – a family-oriented friend who works in construction. The summer fling gets serious, and Jane invites Kenji to live with her in Honolulu. Passion will soon turn to grief, when a tsunami devastates Hilo and Kenji rushes back to assist. A traumatised Jane can’t face the life that has been swept away, leading to an estrangement between them.

Some of the novel’s most sensitive writing describes how Jane and Kenji tentatively re-establish contact years later and discover their true feelings about a love derailed. Everything to the Sea is a nuanced literary romance, with lively, well-observed characterisation, understated humour, and a narrative that draws force from the conflict of values between the lovers. Reconciliation is a vital theme, and it’s embedded within a piercing portrayal of the pain and struggle of community recovery in the aftermath of a catastrophic event.

Mother Waters by Lisa Nan Joo (Affirm Press, $35)A subgenre of feminist gothic cli-fi has emerged lately. Books in this vein feature a strong female protagonist (usually a scientist) embarking on a survival adventure; they tend to take place in extreme natural environments, with flickers of the numinous haunting the action. Where Charlotte McConaghy’s Wild Dark Shore did it with subantarctic islands, Lisa Nan Joo descends into the lightless depths of the ocean.

Mother Waters follows Charlie, a bioacoustic specialist who has lost herself in marriage. Walking out on her husband on their fifth wedding anniversary, she rededicates herself to a career exploring the sounds of life beneath the waves, even as she remains haunted by her father’s death. He was lost at sea when she was a girl, and his memory is one ghost lying in wait on a planned deep-sea expedition. Funded by a billionaire’s son, Dexter, who’s battling his own father’s difficult legacy, the mission will descend into the otherworldly refuge of an oceanic trench. It’s an unsettling odyssey, marrying psychological and political obstacles (especially those facing women in science) to the greater problems caused by our war against nature.

The Wild Beneath by Kelly Anderson (Text Publishing, $35)Another title in this subgeneric surge, Kelly Anderson’s The Wild Beneath makes more of a ripple than a splash – despite using another tsunami as a hook. On the Pacific Northwest coast, 20-year-old Annie MacLeod has always been deeply attuned to the sea, yet it will be the source of a disaster that strikes just as adulthood arrives. When a tsunami washes away her parents and much of her hometown, it leaves Annie and her childhood sweetheart, Evan, as survivors. But when Annie saves a strange, mute young man called Walker from the wrack and wreckage, a visceral bond forms between them.

They seem bound by something as ancient as the waves, including a private language: Walker emits a hum that only Annie can hear. A predictable love triangle develops, and it’s the formulaic quality of The Wild Beneath that fails to satisfy. What should be a turbulent coming-of-age romance, awash with trauma and wonder, resorts to uninspired prose and superficial characterisation, and the book’s uneven pacing and tone can make its wildness seem rather tame.

The Perfect Circle by Claudia Petrucci (Wakefield Press, $35)Italian author Claudia Petrucci’s The Perfect Circle is a pleasingly patterned feminist ghost story. A real estate agent, Irene, is called upon for a hard sell. The “round house” on Via Saterna in Milan is known for its circular staircase and interiors, despite its square facade. It’s also haunted by a woman, Lidia, who’s reputed to have died there. Reports of her death may be exaggerated, and the novel unfolds in dual timelines – one moving towards death, one towards new life – as Irene begins to expose the secrets of the haunted house, and the twisted geometries of space and time combine to disorienting effect.

The Perfect Circle creates an escalating sense of unease: the haunted house trope here is a vehicle for exploring gaps between the illusion and reality of women’s experience over everything from romantic love to motherhood. It’s a ghost story that also bears a fascinating resemblance to high-concept detective metafiction – to Borgesian labyrinths, say, or the existential architectural horror of Mark Z. Danielewski’s House of Leaves.

But Won’t I Miss Me by Tiffany Tsao (HarperVia, $35)When it comes to satirising the social expectations of women regarding pregnancy and motherhood, no plot device could be too outrageous. Tiffany Tsao hits upon a sensational speculative trick. In the world of But Won’t I Miss Me, new mothers gain superhuman powers in the final stage of delivery – the “Rebirth” – in which they spawn a “fetal mother”. This doppelganger is identical to the mother, rapidly grows to adult size, and promptly cannibalises and replaces them with a new self – indestructible, ideally maternal, and with an endless (and renewable) supply of energy.

All perfectly normal, except to Vivi, whose Rebirth goes awry, leaving her weakened by postpartum depression. To save herself and her child, Vivi must flee to an uncle and an underworld that society has left behind. She becomes an electrician to serve people who have gone off-grid, and dystopian answers loom to the question of what happened to Vivi during her pregnancy. Tsao’s idea is a brilliant one. True, the world-building isn’t always as well executed as this speculative feminist parable deserves, but it should attract a wide audience with its unflinching critique of the pressures of motherhood.

Dear Son by Thomas Mayo (Hardie Grant, $35)In 2021, when the first edition of this book was published, Thomas Mayo was confident that racism was on the wane. Travelling the country to take the Uluru Statement from the Heart to the wider community, he’d been struck by the positivity. Everything changed, however, when the Nationals and the Liberals announced they opposed the Voice referendum. A torrent of hatred was unleashed. Despite this dark event and the shadow of intergenerational trauma, these letters by Indigenous men to their fathers or their sons are suffused with love and compassion.

At the same time, the history that shaped them and their fathers is never far from the surface. Stan Grant writes of the “deep well of pain” he saw in his father’s eyes. And how glad he is that life has been easier for his son. “Writing to you,” says Mayo to his son, “has been like an antidote for the vestiges of toxic masculinity learnt from father figures, peers and Western culture. I’m still unlearning.” These soul-searching letters are a soulful reckoning with what it means to be a First Nations father and son.

Three Shocks by George Megalogenis (Penguin, $37)Alfred Deakin, our second prime minister, declared that he would “have no traffic with the unclean thing” of “coloured immigration”. When George Megalogenis was growing up in Melbourne in the 1960s and ’70s, this attitude lingered in the playground where he was called “dirty” because of his olive skin. Even as a boy, he sensed that this was an argument about belonging: “Australia’s perpetual agony of identity”.

While most of Three Shocks is political and demographic analysis, this brief foray into memoir captures the origins of Megalogenis’ attunement to the changes in the make-up of our society in recent decades and his insights into how our politicians are lagging the electorate. Migrants and their children now constitute the majority of the Australian population – this is the first shock. The second is that professional women now outnumber blue-collar men in the workforce. The third concerns uncertainty in global alliances and Australians’ wariness of the US and China. Having drilled down into the data and surveyed shifts in the body politic, Megalogenis distils powerful trends that politicians would be wise to heed.

Wild Hope by Claire Scobie (NewSouth, $37)Claire Scobie calls it her “ecophony”. An epiphany of the ecological variety. Ordinary people can wait for governments to “do something” about the urgent crises of our times, she realised, or they can instigate change themselves. As a storyteller, Scobie set out to find the innovators who were showing how things can be done differently. The term that underpins all their stories is “regenerative thinking”.

For farmers Dianne and Ian Haggerty, this means taking infertile land and creating a drought-resistant, chemical-free ecosystem for crops and top-grade wool. For Regen Melbourne, it’s about being the “engine” for the community collaboration behind the push to make the Yarra fit for swimming and for the creatures that live in it. Scobie’s own story binds these hopeful stories together as she moves with her husband, Gumbaynggirr man Aden Ridgeway, to his Country on the mid-north coast of NSW, and discovers what regeneration might mean in her own life.

God AI by Toby Walsh (La Trobe University Press, $37)Toby Walsh’s work Faking It: Artificial Intelligence in a Human World, published in 2023, was fun. It left you feeling alert and informed, but not alarmed. With this book, the twinkle has gone out of his eye. It’s a testament to how quickly things are evolving in this field that Walsh is now deeply concerned about the threats posed by AI. Having dedicated his life to the dream of AI making the world a better place, he is confronted by a growing mood of doom coming from within the industry. Those who are behind AI’s rapid development are now talking about its potential to wipe us all out. (Bizarrely, they are still going full steam ahead.)

Walsh presents a range of possible scenarios from a future in which AI addresses climate change, makes quality healthcare accessible for all and improves everyone’s standards of living, to super-intelligent, God-like AI going rogue with nuclear or biological weapons. Everything hinges on whether humanity can act before it is too late. You might want to fortify yourself with a stiff drink before reading.

Screen Wise by Madonna King (Murdoch Books, $35)When her children were young, Madonna King held their hands when crossing busy roads to protect them from danger. For the same reason, she chose to monitor their smartphones when the time came. Not all parents believe this is the best route, King says. What matters, though, is whether they are proactive, open and involved in helping their children set boundaries on screen time, encouraging critical thinking and teaching them how to develop their identities offline.

Children’s digital lives have long-term effects on brain development, physical health and social and emotional wellbeing. On top of this, there’s the question of how to tackle the possibility of exposure to pornography, sexual extortion and deepfakes, and how to deal with the complexities of AI. Full of useful tips, informative research and stories from the digital frontline, Screen Wise is a valuable guide for parents and children on how to navigate this daunting and ever-morphing terrain.

What else is happening in the book world?

‘It’s huge’: Nike deal breaks new ground in WSL for London City Lionesses

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 21:33:17 GMT

Club owner says deal is largest in women’s game

Claimed to exceed some men’s Premier League shirt deals

The Women’s Super League club London City Lionesses’ new front-of-shirt sponsorship deal with Nike is the largest in the women’s game, according to their American owner, Michele Kang.

The length and value of the deal has not been disclosed but sources close to the WSL club are hailing it as a gamechanging moment and Kang claims that it even exceeds some men’s Premier League clubs’ shirt deals.

London City, who host Manchester United on Friday in the opening game of the new WSL campaign, are about to embark on only their second top-flight season, but this summer they have shocked the sport by signing a flurry of some of the biggest names in women’s football, including the former Ballon d’Or winner Alexia Putellas, the former England goalkeeper Mary Earps and Putellas’ Spain and Barcelona teammate, Mapi León.

It has been reported that the largest current front-of-shirt sponsorship deal for a women’s football team is an approximately $4m per year agreement reached by the new NWSL franchise in Atlanta – who will begin competing in 2028, but Kang told BBC Sport: “I can absolutely confirm that this is the largest women-only front-of-shirt deal. It is higher than the Atlanta number.

“I can absolutely also share that it is higher than some of the men’s Premier League front-of-shirt deals. It’s huge. That’s why it is landmark. There are so many other people who believe in the future of women’s football. They [Nike] didn’t make this decision lightly. They did not write a charity cheque. They believe in the future and they believe together we will invest and build this future together.”

The deal will be a major boost to London City’s finances. In their most recent set of financial accounts, they posted an annual revenue of just £902,000 for the 2024-25 season, when they won promotion to the top flight. Their operating loss was over £10m, and more than 10 times that revenue.

Their transfer business has attracted questions about how they can fit their lavish spending within the salary cap, as the WSL’s rules dictate that clubs cannot spend more on their player wage bills than 80% of their relevant revenue plus up to £4m of owner contributions. But it is understood this Nike deal will transform their annual revenue astronomically compared to previous seasons.

JD Vance reacts to airstrike that killed four at Iran wedding: ‘Things happen’

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 21:04:18 GMT

US vice-president says he’s ‘extremely skeptical’ of Iran reports when asked whether US was responsible for deaths

The US vice-president, JD Vance, said “sometimes things happen” when asked on Thursday whether an American strike was responsible for killing four people, including a child, at a wedding celebration in southern Iran this week.

The strike hit Kuhestak, a town in Sirik county on the strait of Hormuz. The toll was reported not by the Iranian government but by the Iranian Red Crescent, a member of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement that operates independently of Tehran and is generally treated by international monitors as a credible source on casualty figures.

Asked at a White House press briefing whether the US was responsible, Vance dismissed the reporting.

“I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far, so I’m extremely skeptical of this,” he said, offering no acknowledgment that the killings had been confirmed by an internationally recognized humanitarian body.

“What I can say with 100% confidence is that, unlike the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC, the United States never targets civilians in combat,” Vance continued. “We never will do that. We never have done that, and unfortunately, obviously, sometimes things happen.”

Vance told reporters that he had no new information on the specific strike, but that the US was investigating and, unlike Iran, learns from its mistakes.

He also said that the conflict between the US and Iran, which has now stretched into a seventh month, and led to the deaths of 18 US service members, was not presently “a war”. The comment sparked immediate backlash from Democrats and critics.

“It’s unbelievable gaslighting,” Congressman Ro Khanna, a Democrat of California, said in a video posted to X.

“This is war,” he added. “You know who understands it’s a war? Donald Trump. He claims that we’re winning the war.”

Earlier on Thursday, Trump claimed in a social media post that the US had “virtually unlimited” amounts of mid- to high-grade munitions, and called journalists who have reported on the Pentagon’s dwindling stockpiles “treasonous SCUM”.

The remarks come amid a broader US-Iran war that continues with no sign of a lasting peace despite months of halting negotiations.

The US and Iran exchanged fire earlier this week, renewing fears of greater escalation across the region. US Central Comman (Centcom) has said the broader strike package that Tuesday night targeted Iranian air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and communications facilities, without specifying whether the wedding venue was among the intended targets. The Red Crescent said shrapnel from the US missile strike hit the residential home where the wedding celebration was under way, killing four people and wounding more than 50 others.

Iranian authorities have previously put the overall death toll from US and Israeli strikes in the thousands, figures that outside observers, including US-based monitoring groups, have broadly corroborated.

The strike also revives scrutiny of a 28 February US attack roughly 23 miles away, in Minab, that hit a school compound and killed at least 156 people, most of them schoolchildren. A preliminary US military inquiry reportedly found that strike resulted from a targeting error, after outdated coordinates identified the school as part of an adjacent Revolutionary Guard naval base. The Pentagon said at the time it was investigating; a full report has not been made public.

Reform officials ‘plotted to break law on foreign donations’ in undercover film

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 21:01:51 GMT

Investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News shows man posing as ‘impermissible donor’ paying for polling that helped Reform

Nigel Farage is facing fresh criticism on the eve of the Reform UK party conference after some of his team were filmed appearing to plot to avoid electoral laws on foreign donations in an undercover investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News.

A group of investigative journalists called Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party.

The polling was not attributed to Reform, and was reported in the Telegraph and the Times without those newspapers knowing that it was commissioned by the party and paid for by the US donor. The benefit in kind was also not reported to the Electoral Commission.

In footage of another meeting, a senior adviser to Farage, Dan Jukes, appeared to suggest to the fake UK-based supporter that his US-based father could make a substantial donation by channelling it through the son.

When the possible structure was explained to Farage, footage of a meeting between him and the fake donors shows him saying: “Thank you both.”

The investigation will reopen intense scrutiny of Reform’s approach to donations and its finances, which are already the subject of a standards inquiry and police investigation.

Reform said it had been “the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded climate-change activists posing as would-be party donors” and the party denied any wrongdoing.

In Channel 4 News’ investigation, broadcast on Thursday night, footage shows that the fake UK-based supporter also had conversations with Reform UK’s head of policy, James Orr, who talked about commissioning polling that would be paid for by the US-based father.

In the film, Orr can be heard saying of the arrangement that Farage “doesn’t know, won’t know” and it was the kind of thing he would “rather not know”. At one point the footage shows him saying it was “totally legit” and with “nothing untowards about it at all”.

Farage was subsequently caught on camera in a meeting with the fake US donor in Clacton where he appears to be celebrating the success of the poll, saying it was “amazing” and provided “bang for buck”, adding: “It worked. Boom.”

Jukes, a close aide to Farage, was also filmed meeting the fake donor, and at a Reform UK reception where in one conversation he appeared to introduce the undercover operative as “key donor for off-the-book project”.

In footage of a meeting with the fake US donor, he is heard describing the polling as “clandestine” and “hugely important”.

The polling, conducted by JL Partners, made headlines before the local elections in May. The foreign source of funding and its links to Reform were not publicly disclosed, and the Telegraph said it had now suspended the articles about the polling, while the Times said it was not aware of the relationship with Reform.

After Channel 4 News’ broadcast, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said the “scandal goes right to the top of Reform UK”. She added: “Nigel Farage needs to urgently prove today that his top team haven’t broken the law and secretly plotted to undermine our democracy.”

Ed Davey, the leader of the Liberal Democrats, called on the police and the Electoral Commission to investigate.

A Reform spokesperson said: “Reform UK has a robust vetting process for prospective donors approved by the Electoral Commission. The hoaxers are ‘Verbatim Investigations’; a new company, incorporated in July 2026 in an attempt to mask their true identity: the Centre for Climate Reporting.”

The party claimed the group’s methods had previously been “rebuked by members of the United States Congress” for “videos [that] appear to be substantially edited, creating an incomplete record of the conversation”.

The investigation is likely to create a serious problem for Farage as he attempts to turn the page on Reform’s summer of funding scandals, with his party conference speech scheduled for Friday.

In the speech, he will boast of record donations compared with the other parties, including £4m from a crypto billionaire pardoned by Donald Trump in the last quarter.

The Reform UK leader will tell the annual Birmingham gathering that the party is “much stronger than we were last year”, saying that it has the highest number of members and has brought in the most donations.

The party outperformed Labour and the Conservatives with donations of more than £5m in the second quarter of this year, new figures from the Electoral Commission show.

However, it remains reliant on a handful of mega-donors who have been based abroad and could be caught by the government’s new £100,000 annual cap on overseas funders which requires donors to have been a UK resident for 12 months.

The biggest donation in the last few months was the £4m from Ben Delo, a crypto entrepreneur who has been based in Hong Kong in recent years but in April said he was moving back to the UK.

Delo, who was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money-laundering controls in his cryptocurrency business, before being pardoned by Trump, has previously given Reform £4m.

Party sources said it was “very confident” that none of Delo’s latest £4m would need to be returned due to the cap when the legislation is passed.

The government has said donors would have to have been on the UK electoral register for at least 12 months and meet a residency test showing that they are “genuinely resident at a UK address”.

Any gifts over the £100,000 cap from an overseas-based donor would have to be handed back once the new legislation is passed if deemed to be impermissible under the new law.

Reform’s confidence in the donation would suggest Delo has been on the UK domestic electoral register and believes he could meet the residency test when the donations were made in April and May. Delo did not respond to a request for comment.

Christopher Harborne, the Thailand-based billionaire who has given the party £15m and £5m to Farage personally, did not give any cash after the cap was introduced in March.

The £5m gift to Farage from before the last election is under investigation by the standards commissioner, and Reform has slid in the polls since the amount was first revealed by the Guardian.

Nessun Dolore review – sketchy Roman fable of liberal white guilt

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 20:00:47 GMT

Venice film festivalA white man’s eyes are opened to cruelty and racism when a young boy is thrust into his life in Gianni Amelio’s bold but ultimately naive drama

From the heart of Rome, and broadly in an Italian tradition of sentimentalist realism, film-maker Gianni Amelio brings us a fairytale of the city, about the liberal white guilt of those who live a prosperous pain-free existence and those whom Frantz Fanon called the wretched of the earth.

There is some incidental interest and the film is beautifully shot, but finally it buckles under the weight of its own preposterousness and naivety. It is also sketchy about how and why people go into and come out of prison; the final shot, a supposedly heartwarming visionary moment of redemption and reconciliation, looks absurd.

Davide is a secondhand book dealer with a little-visited stall: who on earth reads books nowadays? He is played by Alessandro Borghi with something of that troubled decency that Peter Sarsgaard often projects. Evidently, Davide has got enough family money (and a handsome book-lined flat) that he doesn’t have to worry about sales. He flirts with a literature professor (Valeria Golino) but doesn’t quite have the maturity to pursue a relationship.

Davide’s world falls apart one day when he is approached in the street by a north African man (Ramzi Lafrindi) – perhaps a migrant or asylum seeker – hand-in-hand with a nine-year-old boy (Beidja Yahiaoui), whom he is clearly trying to be rid of. This man shoves the small boy into Davide’s arms, insisting that he is Davide’s responsibility.

Is he? Or is this a desperate stratagem on the man’s part, gambling that there are enough white men nursing guilty sexual secrets for this ruse to have a chance of succeeding? Either way, the kid follows the increasingly alarmed Davide around, until he furiously orders the boy to back off, which he does, off the pavement, with terrible results.

From there, Davide embarks on an odyssey of guilt and shame, red-pilled by his close encounter with poverty, his eyes opened to cruelty and racism, visiting the shantytown quarters where poor migrants are to be found and makes a muddied and disastrous attempt to open his heart and his flat.

It is a bold and interesting high-concept premise – though audiences might have been expecting more twists and turns in the narrative. In the end, the film settles for a placid sense of personal unhappiness and self-forgiveness on the hero’s part, which supersedes any larger sense of poverty or injustice in society.

Nessun Dolore screened at the Venice film festival.

We’re prepared to change the law to reform water industry, says Angela Eagle

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 19:49:34 GMT

Exclusive: New environment secretary insists ‘nothing is off the table’ in dealing with ailing Thames Water

Britain’s insolvency laws cannot deal with the aggressive behaviour shown by the companies that control Thames Water, the environment secretary has said, as she confirmed ministers were prepared to take it into public ownership.

Angela Eagle told the Guardian she was determined to reform the water industry after being told by Andy Burnham to make it her top priority.

But she warned that could mean a change in law to factor in the way in which the US hedge funds that own much of Thames Water have kept it running while seeking a deal to renegotiate its debts.

The battle over Thames looks set to become the first test of the prime minister’s determination to bring Britain’s utilities into public control even in the face of concerted corporate lobbying and the threat of legal action.

In her first big interview since becoming environment secretary, Eagle said putting Thames Water into special administration – a likely first step to deprivatisation – could prove more complicated than some activists think.

“A lot of people think you can just choose [special administration] … [but] you either are, or you aren’t, insolvent. And whatever people think of Thames at the moment, it isn’t technically insolvent,” she said.

“The Water Act didn’t really envisage this kind of behaviour and this kind of corporate presence behaving in particular ways.

“But we have a water bill coming along, and nothing is off the table. We’ve got a legislative vehicle coming along soon to enable us to do what we decide to do.”

Burnham has repeatedly promised to take public utilities into public control, focusing especially on energy and water. He told the Guardian before becoming MP for Makerfield that he intended to nationalise Thames.

The prime minister’s focus on utilities puts Eagle at the centre of much of what he is trying to do in government, including reforming the water industry and cleaning up illegal dumping sites.

She is taking part in weekly meetings of the National Drought Group, which is coordinating the response to the country’s fifth drought in three years.

Speaking from Havant Thicket in Hampshire, which is due to be the country’s first new reservoir since 1992, she said the country had become less resilient under previous governments and she would speed up the pace of new infrastructure.

“The system has got more clogged up,” she said, comparing the situation with the one she faced as a minister in the governments of Tony Blair and Gordon Brown.

“Trying to get anything done from start to finish is now much slower, much more difficult. It seems to somehow be that people always give you loads of reasons why you can’t do anything, rather than [saying] strategically, we need nine reservoirs or this reservoir, or whatever the infrastructure is.”

One of her first tasks will be to decide what to do about Thames Water, which is struggling under a £20bn debt pile and has been given a record £122.7m fine for sewage spills and unlawful shareholder payouts.
