Gloria Steinem, groundbreaking feminist campaigner, dies aged 92

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 16:42:35 GMT

Prolific author campaigned against domestic violence, female genital mutilation, pornography and the Vietnam and Gulf wars

‘We badly need to raise our boys more like our girls’: Gloria Steinem – a life in quotes

Hillary Clinton leads tributes to Gloria Steinem: ‘Her activism was rooted in optimism’

Gloria Steinem, the American feminist and journalist whose activism helped push through greater rights for women around the world has died, aged 92.

Steinem “passed away peacefully at her home in New York City, surrounded by some of the many who loved her”, a statement shared to her Instagram page said.

“Gloria’s near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end,” the post added. “Gloria’s greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard. Her words, actions, and example gave people permission to be their truest selves.”

Steinem brought a feminist perspective into the mainstream through rigorous journalism, public speaking and activism. The author of nine books, she campaigned against domestic violence, female genital mutilation, the pornography industry and the Vietnam and Gulf wars. She also worked in support of causes including Black Lives Matter, the reunification of Korea, female reproductive rights, LGBTQ+ rights and the Times Up movement. In 1984, she was arrested while protesting against apartheid outside the South African embassy in Washington DC.

Outside Steinem’s elegant, classic townhouse in Manhattan’s Upper East Side neighbourhood on Thursday morning, passersby left tributes.

Debbie Goldberg, who said she lived close by, placed a bunch of red flowers next to the steps up to the front door.

“I’ve never done that before. But she deserved it,” she said, describing Steinem as one of the most influential people for women’s rights and human rights in history.

“She’s a hero to all women whether they know it or not,” she said.

Goldberg said that she saw Steinem speak in Washington DC “around 30 years ago”, and then bumped into her as they were both heading into a cinema a few blocks away to see the Barbie movie in 2023. Goldberg said had been planning to watch Steinem speak in a few weeks’ time at a YMCA close by. “She’s always been an idol of mine,” Goldberg added.

Others left a bouquet of roses mixed with a variety of blooms in pink and white, and a large seashell filled with gems and other trinkets.

Born in Ohio in 1934, Steinem grew up in a trailer home. Her mother’s mental illness left her struggling to hold on to work and in and out of sanatoriums. When she was 10, her parents separated and, while growing up in a rundown home in Toledo with her mother, Steinem began to notice the hostility her mother endured as a working woman.

After graduating from a women’s liberal arts college in 1956, Steinem travelled to India for two years, where she worked as a legal clerk in the country’s supreme court. Returning to the US, she worked as the director of the Independent Research Service, a CIA front that recruited American students to disrupt the Soviet-controlled World Youth Festivals in Vienna and Helsinki. Steinem later revealed she had always known who was bankrolling the operation: “If I had a choice I would do it again.”

In 1962, she received her first “serious assignment” in journalism from the Esquire magazine editor, Clay Felker. Her feature on contraception, The Moral Disarmament of Betty Coed, detailed how women were forced to choose between careers and family. The following year, Steinem went undercover as a Playboy Bunny for 11 days, to write her infamous, two-part exposé of how the glamour models were treated while working in Hugh Hefner’s Playboy Club. Forced into tight costumes and high heels, Steinem lost 10lb – half of them in a single night – during her stint; her manager celebrated by making her costume two inches tighter. Following the article, she was unable to get work because “because I had now become a Bunny – and it didn’t matter why”.

In 1968, Felker hired her to work at New York magazine, in which she would coin the term “reproductive freedom” for an article about an abortion “speakout” in Greenwich Village. Having had an abortion in London when was 22, she later described feeling a “big click” while at the protest and said the day marked the start of her life as an “active feminist”.

“I think the person who said: ‘Honey, if men could get pregnant, abortion would be a sacrament’ was right,” she told the Observer in 2011. “Speaking for myself, I knew it was the first time I had taken responsibility for my own life. I wasn’t going to let things happen to me. I was going to direct my life, and therefore it felt positive.”

She also credited black feminists including Florynce Kennedy, Evelyn Cunningham, Shirley Chisholm and Fannie Lou Hamer for teaching her the importance of activism. “It was like finding a family,” she said of that time. “As wildly different as we may be, and we certainly were, women share hopes and a certain vision of the world, and a certain shit detector.”

This also began Steinem’s career as a provocative journalist, penning articles including If Men Could Menstruate, which ran in Ms, a magazine co-founded by Steinem and Dorothy Pitman Hughes in 1971. The first issue featured Wonder Woman on the cover; the superhero had recently given up her powers to stay with her male love interest, and the essay argued that DC Comics should restore her powers and return the character to her feminist roots. Steinem also wrote articles such as What It Would Be Like If Women Win in Time, and After Black Power, Women’s Liberation, the 1969 New York magazine article that would make her name as a feminist leader.

Terrified of public speaking and conflict, but media savvy, Steinem used the platform she gained as a white, educated woman to speak out for those traditionally ignored – black people, ethnic minorities and the working class. Sex and race were always intertwined, she argued in 1971, “because they are easy, and visible differences have been the primary ways of organising human beings into superior and inferior groups and into the cheap labour on which this system still depends.” In 2017, she said: “It doesn’t surprise me that the most virulent anti-abortion measures are coming from Alabama and other southern states because racism and sexism are always intertwined. You can’t perpetuate racism without controlling women and reproduction.”

Steinem was also a polarising figure. Some feminists felt her position as a public leader in the movement had been decided not by merit but by the media, which chose her for being young, white and attractive; in her 2015 book My Life on the Road, she wrote that the “idea that whatever I had accomplished was all about looks would remain a biased and hurtful accusation even into my old age”.

She was roundly criticised for decades for a 1998 opinion piece for the New York Times, in which she supported President Bill Clinton in the face of sexual harassment allegations. “He is not guilty of sexual harassment,” she wrote, only “a gross, dumb, and reckless pass at a supporter during a low point in her life”. In 2017, she said: “We have to believe women. I wouldn’t write the same thing now because there’s probably more known about other women now.” She was also regarded as hostile to transgender rights because of a piece she wrote in 1977, a position she clarified in 2013: “I believe that transgender people, including those who have transitioned, are living out real, authentic lives. Those lives should be celebrated, not questioned.”

In 1986, Steinem was diagnosed with breast cancer, then in 1994 the chronic pain condition trigeminal neuralgia. After years of dismissing marriage, she married the environmental activist David Bale in 2000, and remained close with her stepson, the actor Christian Bale, after his father’s death in 2003.

Having supported Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign, Steinem was a prominent critic of Donald Trump, co-chairing and speaking at the Women’s March on Washington, a mass protest held the day after the Trump’s inauguration in January 2017. “The only good news of Trump is that the galvanising of activism is like nothing I have ever seen in my life,” she told the Guardian that year. “A thousand times more even than the Vietnam war, and how important that was – or of any other thing I’ve ever seen.”

In 2011, she told the Observer: “I hope to live to 100. There is so much to do.”

Anna Betts contributed reporting from New York

Of all the epithets thrown at a new prime minister, “people-pleaser” bounces off Andy Burnham. After all, the polls have him with a favourability rating of +13, making him the only party leader who scores above zero. His manner as he responded to all 125 of his questioners on his first Commons appearance this week had a warmth and empathy that his predecessor lacked. It’s a natural timbre, a good bedside manner for an uneasy country.

Keir Starmer’s rating as he left office was -36. He was defenestrated precisely because of his unpopularity. That baffled his allies, but his ratings crashed early into an electoral death zone from which no leader returns. His revenge comes in giving Labour a potentially awkward byelection confrontation with Zack Polanski: although, just as Burnham defeated the right in Makerfield, any candidate under his leadership stands a good chance of defeating the Greens in Holborn and St Pancras.

Starmer’s fall began soon after Labour’s landslide victory in July 2024 with his message of foreboding gloom in the Downing Street garden. The country faced an economic and societal “black hole”, he said, adding that “things will get worse before they get better”.

Burnham has avoided that kind of misery, on Tuesday making a promise to “unlock a feeling of positivity and possibility” in every part of the country. And why not? Hope is always better than despair. It has its own elevating power that can stimulate growth, social optimism and investment. Even in the face of coming storms, it’s better by far to have a leader who raises spirits in adversity.

The strongest El Niño on record, exacerbated by the stresses of the climate emergency, will hit the UK with tempestuously alarming weather through to early 2027. Equally alarming was that, even as Burnham spoke, the bond markets set off their own El Niño with their global sell-off raising interest rates across the world, especially on UK debt. Their preference for investing in AI companies over governments may be the wrong bet, amid warnings of this bubble bursting to the devastation of the global economy. And still there is no sign that Donald Trump will end his calamitous war with Iran and free the world from its economic blight.

Burnham, well-seasoned in the ways of politics, is fully armed against the cannonades from right and left. He’s all too familiar with the particular poison of most of the British press, for ever hostile to Labour. But the extra lashings of vitriol suggests the right are alarmed by his popularity. Here’s Tim Stanley, the Telegraph’s parliamentary sketch writer, on Burnham’s first Commons outing: “What a relief! The PM’s a dud. For a horrid moment I thought Labour had found a man who could flog socialism to simpletons, but Our Andy’s debut at the Dispatch Box – billed as make-or-break for the British Left – was met by embarrassed silence.”

Presumably, it reassures Telegraph readers to be fed exaggeration when both Reform UK and the Conservatives are on the slide. Farage is not recovering from the scrutiny over his astounding £5m gift, while the Tories languish even below their 2024 election result, which was their lowest since 1832.

They perk up at Kemi Badenoch becoming a little less unpopular. She is indeed more confident at PMQs, but her negative rating suggests she’s no people-pleaser. She leads her party downwards. My hunch is it’s not terminal: the Tories always resurrect, but only by shape-shifting to catch up with changing times, from which they periodically disconnect. But it won’t happen under her. Burnham is lucky to have an opponent swimming hard against the modern tide. Until the Tories repent, or at least recognise the catastrophic consequences of their Brexit, they won’t revive. Their anti-net zero climate extremism is bizarrely out of tune with a country that has just seen record heatwaves and which, Tory voters included, backs the zero emissions target.

Her “slashing” Britain’s welfare bill may be what people want, but it also acts as a reminder of the sheer cruelty of the Tories’ austerity years. And she is prone to tumbling into her own elephant traps. She thought she had a gotcha when she challenged Burnham as a spendthrift: what had he cut? “Tax is the simple answer,” he said, quick as a flash, citing two tax cuts in his first week.

His summer of goodwill defied Labour’s enemies, who enjoyed little success opposing capping bus fares at £2, scrapping the 5% VAT on energy bills or the creation of No 10 North, all of which were well received by the public. They will hope his pledge to end rough sleeping in England by Christmas fails. When faced with the prison overcrowding crisis, he did the unpopular thing and released prisoners. Unwelcome public advice from friends, including his former economic adviser Jim O’Neill, warning he must make cuts or tax rises has been picked up with glee by Badenoch. But oddly, she failed to mention his solution: end the ruinous triple lock on pensions.

Many people are pleased that he will set about capping political donations. Stella Creasy withdrew her strongly backed amendment to the representation of the people bill calling for a £500,000 cap, signalling her confidence in Burnham’s promised taskforce to draw up a plan. That’s a people-pleaser for a public disgusted with the squalor of cash swirling around Westminster. Another strongly backed amendment from Alex Sobel, to set up a national commission on electoral reform, was ruled out of the scope of the bill by the speaker, but the government confirmed it supports reform: it will be back and in the next manifesto.

That’s a good start. You couldn’t hope for better. Can he buck the trend of prime ministers haemorrhaging popularity within months? Storms ahead are threatening. But facing into the wind with optimism is the way to go.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

Do people really smell different as they get older? The truth behind ‘old person smell’

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 16:00:42 GMT

Experts say that the smell comes from a chemical compound called 2-nonenal, and it can show up much earlier than one expects

Last week, my mom complained that she’s starting to smell “like an old person”.

She had grabbed her favorite sweater and draped it over herself at the movie theater. “It smelled like my grandmother,” she said, almost whispering. “I thought someone must have borrowed the jacket. But it was just me.”

My mom, who’s in her 60s, has a ton of energy. Her hair is thick and still naturally chestnut. She’s healthy and strong; she likes to hike and go to rock concerts.

“I don’t feel like an old person. Why do I smell like one?” she whined.

I told her, truthfully, that I didn’t notice any new aroma. I thought she smelled the same as always: a mix of lotion and gardenia. But I immediately knew what she was talking about.

Experts say that we do smell different as we age. “It’s one of the most universal, least talked-about parts of being human,” says Dr Roya Javid, a dermatologist in Monterey, California. “It’s just biology, unfolding on schedule, the same way we grow taller, then our hair goes gray. Every single person on the planet goes through these same transitions.”

The musty odor that people sometimes call “old person smell” comes from a chemical compound called 2-nonenal. 2-nonenal is produced when certain skin oils oxidize and break down, says Javid.

It’s a normal – and unavoidable – change.

“Our skin is coated in a thin layer of natural oils called skin lipids. They keep skin soft, waterproof and protected,” she says. Those lipids are made up of fatty acids, and as we age, the fatty acids change in composition. At the same time, the skin’s ability to fight off every day wear-and-tear slows down. The oils are more exposed, and when they break down through oxidation, they release 2-nonenal.

“It’s just a natural byproduct of skin ageing – not dirt, not poor hygiene,” Javid says. “It’s just oil quietly changing over time, the same way metal changes when it’s exposed to air.”

Levels of 2-nonenal vary by person. “We don’t yet know why some develop a stronger scent than others,” says Javid. “Though an individual’s skin-oil composition, genetics, the skin’s microbiome, hygiene practices, clothing, health and environment may all play a role in both how much 2-nonenal is produced and how much stays on the skin throughout the day.”

Experts say “old person smell” can show up much earlier than you might expect.

A Japanese study from 2001 tested the skin of subjects between the ages of 26 and 75, and detected 2-nonenal starting at age 40. But Dr Arshad Rather, consultant geriatrician and general physician at Medical Express Clinic in London, says this doesn’t mean people wake up with a noticeable new odor.

“Research suggests 2-nonenal increases gradually the older you get, particularly past middle age. It’s not a switch flipping at 40 – more a dial slowly turning up,” says Rather.

Experts note that developing an age-specific odor isn’t unique to older adults. In fact, every age group has associated smells, for better or worse.

“Every stage of life has its own signature scent,” says Javid. “Babies smell sweet and milky because their scent glands haven’t switched on yet. Puberty flips that switch, and suddenly hormones drive a stronger, muskier smell for teens. Adulthood has a more consistent scent tied to sweat and daily life. And [these] changes in the skin’s natural oils give people a different scent later on.”

Any negative feelings people have toward “old person smell” are really a perception problem, not a reality problem, Javid says.

A blind test found that the 2-nonenal scent may not be disagreeable. In one 2012 study, researchers asked 41 young adults to smell T-shirts worn by individuals from three age groups: young (20–30 years old), middle-age (45–55) and old age (75–95). The researchers found that the odor from older adults was “rated as less intense and less unpleasant” than other groups.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

Dr Johan N Lundström, a professor of psychology at Karolinska Institutet in Sweden and one of the authors of the study, says his team was surprised by the results. They hypothesized that smell would follow a linear trend, with the youngest group being rated highest and the oldest group rated the lowest, but that wasn’t the case.

“The elderly have a clearly separate body odor quality, but it was not rated as being all that negative,” Dr Lundström says.

Experts say there’s no way to stop 2-nonenal from developing. But there are some ways to manage the odor.

Javid says regular bathing can wash away some of the scent. However, soap and water won’t fully remove the chemical, because it doesn’t simply sit on the surface of the skin like sweat – rather, it’s being generated continuously. Deodorants might temporarily cover up a smell, but won’t remove 2-nonenal.

Meanwhile, regularly washing clothes, sheets and airing out rooms can help reduce the odor in the home. But because 2-nonenal won’t easily wash out, it can linger even after the most dedicated cleaning practices.

Some body wash products are marketed as neutralizing 2-nonenal, such as soap made with persimmon. Experts say while there are some anecdotal accounts that these help, scientific evidence is lacking.

Rather suspects there’s a connection between 2-nonenal production and a person’s lifestyle and diet, but says more studies are needed. “Since the smell comes from an oxidation reaction, reducing oxidative stress is a sensible target. Eating antioxidant-rich foods, such as colourful fruit and vegetables and sources of vitamins C and E, can reduce oxidative stress,” he says.

“Not smoking and protecting your skin from sun damage are sensible anti-oxidation habits too,” adds Rather.

In the end, experts say it’s true that people develop a different smell as they age, but it’s nothing to be embarrassed about.

If a person starts to notice they smell like 2-nonenal – which we all will – Javid urges them to not feel self-conscious or spend a fortune on special soaps.

“Focus on the things that support your skin generally: antioxidants, less sun damage, less smoking, good hydration,” she says. “And know that the science says you’re worrying about something that, objectively, isn’t as bad as the stereotype.”

World Cup wishlists, early movers, big clearouts: 2026 summer transfer window trends

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 16:00:42 GMT

At the end of a busy transfer window which spanned the World Cup, here are some of the subplots of the summer

The World Cup is always a good shop window. Yan Diomande was already a rising star at RB Leipzig but shining for Côte d’Ivoire in the US helped push up his price tag before a £115.7m move to Real Madrid. There were other breakout stars: Switzerland’s Johan Manzambi, whose signature Aston Villa pipped Newcastle to; Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Kerim Alajbegovic, who went to Juventus; and Ghana’s Caleb Yirenkyi, who is now in the Premier League with Coventry. Cape Verde’s cult hero Vozinha now keeps net for the Chilean giants Colo-Colo and Morocco’s attacking dynamo, Ismael Saibari, has rocked up at Bayern. Billy Munday

While Europe’s wealthiest clubs generally allowed the World Cup to run its course before moving for their main targets, there were some exceptions. Real Madrid announced the signing of Marc Cucurella for £52m as he was getting ready to start Spain’s opener against Cape Verde, then Bernardo Silva before Portugal began their campaign two days later. Liverpool spent heavily early on as they signed Víctor Muñoz for £34.5m in mid-June and completed their pre-agreed £60m deal for Jérémy Jacquet at the start of July. Tottenham had spent almost £230m on Jan Paul van Hecke, Mateus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali before the last 16 was over, also adding Andy Robertson and Marcos Senesi on free transfers. Other clubs seemed to treat the World Cup as an opportunity to do deals under the radar. Bayer Leverkusen moved quickly, just as they did in January, to sign promising youngsters in Kennet Eichhorn and Afonso Moreira for a combined £32.8m in June. Brighton were among the most proactive squad builders in the Premier League, spending just over £50m on Zadok Yohanna, Costinha and Pascal Struijk before the World Cup action had moved beyond the last 32. Will Magee

“Think about us like a volcano,” Hull’s owner, Acun Ilicali, said in July. “It’s boiling right now and it’s going to erupt.” He was not wrong. In the end, the promoted Premier League side signed 18 players this summer for a combined sum of £156.5m. Ipswich went even further, splashing £194.7m on 15 additions, while Coventry spent £122.4m on 11 new signings. It is a far cry from a few years ago when many promoted teams were frugal, often relying on the players who took them to the promised land. As recently as 2021 the three promoted teams, Norwich, Watford and Brentford, spent a combined £98.8m – with the latter’s acquisition of Kristoffer Ajer from Celtic the most expensive signing at £13m. The fact that Premier League newcomers are spending so lavishly is a reminder of the division’s financial dominance and the game’s increasingly extreme economic disparities. Marcus Christenson

In sharp contrast to the Premier League, where eight clubs had a net spend over £100m and only six made a net gain, 15 out of 18 Ligue 1 clubs made money on player trading this summer. Paris Saint-Germain led the way thanks in no small part to the £123m deal which took Bradley Barcola to Liverpool, making a net profit of more than £150m overall. Lille, who made around £100m, sanctioned big-money departures for Ayyoub Bouaddi and Matias Fernandez-Pardo, who joined Manchester City and Newcastle for £85.7m and £51m respectively. Strasbourg, the smaller cog in BlueCo’s transfer machine, brought in almost £90m as they moved on Diego Moreira, Julio Enciso, Abdoul Ouattara, Guéla Doué, Valentín Barco and Emmanuel Emegha – the latter two moving to, that’s right, Chelsea. While Ligue 1 has been a conveyor belt of talent for some time, its output is reaching new levels. Of the 15 biggest fees ever received by French clubs, five have come in this window. WM

There has been plenty of upheaval this summer, but nowhere more so than at Fiorentina. After battling relegation for much of last season, eventually finishing 15th in Serie A, the Viola have moved on 34 players either permanently or on loan, with Moise Kean and Tariq Lamptey among the high-profile departees. No other club in Europe’s “big five” leagues can match that but Chelsea, with 33 leavers (18 on loan), are not far off. While Chelsea made a net profit of around £60m thanks to the £125m deadline-day deal for Enzo Fernández, Fiorentina have spent more than £100m net on a rebuild from the ground up. Depending on interpretation, that’s either a sign of Premier League money taking on a bizarre and irrational life of its own, or a lesson in the eye-watering cost of fixing a failed recruitment strategy. Badly parked ebikes in London are a menace – but other cities have shown us the solution

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 15:43:07 GMT

Paris converted tens of thousands of on-street parking spaces into docking stations, fundamentally changing its approach to public space

Agustin Guilisasti is founder and CEO of the London ebike operator Forest

Shared ebikes have become a key part of London’s transport network. From Hounslow to Greenwich, it’s rare to step on to the street without seeing one, and they now facilitate millions of journeys every month. Forest recorded 3m rides this July alone, a new high. Demand keeps rising, and operators are logging ever-higher ride-per-bike ratios, a key measure of how intensively fleets are being used.

This is good news for London, which gains a cleaner, healthier and more sustainable way to get around – one that eases reliance on private car ownership. And, with new research revealing that air-quality improvements driven by the ultra-low emission zone (Ulez) have led to better lung health in children, the benefits of reducing polluting journeys are increasingly clear.

But shared ebikes also draw real criticism. Poorly parked bikes make near-daily headlines, and with good reason. I’m acutely aware of the criticism directed at us and I know this is a problem. Misparked bikes, and the cluttered pavements they leave behind, cause understandable frustration. It’s a nuisance, and – at worst – a genuine hazard for pedestrians and other road users. Especially disabled pedestrians or those with access needs.

But the solution doesn’t lie in fewer bikes – it lies in answering the crucial question around parking. Other European cities have shown that, with the right infrastructure and planning, shared ebikes can be woven into existing transport systems. They’ve done it by answering one key question: where should bikes go when they’re not moving?

London’s cycling infrastructure has come a long way – the Cycleway network now covers 450km (280 miles) – but our roads are still asked to accommodate buses, taxis, pedestrians, scooters, cyclists, private vehicles and mopeds within the same finite space. If London is serious about making shared ebikes part of its transport network, policymakers need to rethink how that space is allocated, particularly when it comes to parking.

Paris offers the clearest case study. The administration of the former mayor, Anne Hidalgo, didn’t just build cycle lanes; it fundamentally reconsidered how public space should be used once the pedalling stops. Her administration converted tens of thousands of on-street car parking spaces into Vélib’ docking stations (Paris’s version of Transport for London’s Santander bike scheme) and dedicated bays for bikes and shared micromobility. These, incidentally, also made room for wider pavements and more trees.

Hidalgo’s approach was informed by a simple insight: a single car parking space can hold about 10 bicycles. Repurposed, that space now serves hundreds of people a day instead of storing one stationary vehicle.

London hasn’t yet had this conversation, but the timing has never been better, for two key reasons. First, car ownership in the capital is declining. Almost half of London households no longer own a car, rising to nearly two-thirds in inner London. Yet about 18% of households in inner London still own two or more vehicles.

And, second, as part of the recently passed English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act, TfL has been tasked with designing a pan-London licensing framework for shared micromobility that will finally bring regulation to a market that has grown rapidly over the past five years. It is inevitable that parking for shared mobility schemes will be a key part of that framework’s design.

I see this scheme’s design as a real opportunity to question whether one of the world’s best-connected cities should keep prioritising scarce street space for second cars, over transport that serves thousands of people every day.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

For example, if the mayor and TfL converted even 15% of the on-street parking currently taken up by second cars into dedicated micromobility bays, this would create space for almost 1m shared ebikes – far more than the estimated 50,000 already in London and far more than we would ever conceivably need – with every one of them parked on the carriageway, not the pavement.

With help from operators, boroughs, TfL and the mayor, London could solve its ebike parking conundrum in an instant and get on with the most urgent task: integrating them into the transport system safely, sustainably and for the benefit of all Londoners.

Agustin Guilisasti is founder and CEO of the London ebike operator Forest

Mike Dean claims he played secret games for a laugh while refereeing matches

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 15:22:39 GMT

Former official says he ‘tried to stay in the centre circle’

Referees’ group thought to be puzzled by remarks

The former Premier League referee Mike Dean claims he used to take part in secret challenges while officiating, including trying to stay in the centre circle for as long as possible, as he confessed to “just joking about” during matches. The remarks, made by one of the most well-known officials in the English game, have been met with bemusement by refereeing officials who say there is no evidence of any such behaviour having ever taken place.

Dean was a member of the select group of referees for more than two decades before he retired in 2022 and a brief spell as a video assistant referee followed. In an interview on Jamie Vardy’s podcast this week, Dean shared anecdotes from his time as a top-flight official in the pre-VAR era. “We used to say, ‘We’ll kick off now. Right, see how long we can go without blowing a whistle,’” he said. “I’ve done that a few times in the Premier League, before VAR obviously – [I] went 20, 25 minutes without blowing a whistle.

“I used to do another thing. I used to stand in the centre circle – see how long I could stay in the centre circle before I had to leave. That was just me joking about. I got about 15 minutes once.”

Officials within the refereeing organisation, Pro Ref, are understood to be puzzled by the claims, with the suggestion that a referee could stay in the centre circle for 15 minutes without someone noticing, for example, seen as highly improbable.

This is not the first time that Dean has courted controversy in a post-retirement interview. Dean was stood down from his role as a VAR in 2023 after failing to intervene over an error in a match between Tottenham and Chelsea, refereed by Anthony Taylor. Describing Taylor as a “mate”, Dean told Simon Jordan’s podcast that he had chosen not to ask Taylor to review his decision on a VAR monitor because he didn’t want him to have “any more grief than he already had”.

Dean earned notoriety during his time as a referee for his flamboyant mannerisms and apparent eye for the camera – as captured in the terrace chant “Mike Dean, it’s all about you”. But he was also held to be one of the best officials in the top flight, taking charge of 561 matches – and issuing a record 114 red cards – over the course of his 22-year career.

Kemi the Valkyrie spoils for a fight and has the Russians in her sights

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 15:08:15 GMT

Tory leader scents Labour weakness on defence spending and declares it’s 2030 or bust

UK politics live – latest updates

There’s something about Kemi Badenoch making a keynote speech – everything she does comes billed as keynote these days – about defence that makes most normal people a little nervous. Because when Kemi talks about defence, what’s really on her mind is war. Starting one, if possible.

Kemi is never happier than when picking a fight. With herself, if no one else is around. You get the feeling that, left on a desert island she would be dreaming of Apocalypse Now. Flying low over the Mekong delta in a helicopter gunship, the Ride of the Valkyries playing through her earphones while she yelled: “I love the smell of napalm in the morning.”

Still, you can’t blame an opposition leader for opportunism. It’s the crumbs they live off. And the Tories reckon they have identified a Labour weakness. John Healey resigned as defence secretary a few months back over Keir Starmer’s reluctance to come up with a plan of spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

Now that Andy Burnham has appointed him chancellor, Healey seems suddenly rather reluctant to make the commitment he was asking of Rachel Reeves. Much happier to be pushed back to the longer-term goal of 3.5% by 2035, with the heavy lifting being done sometime, maybe never, after the next election. There are some decisions politicians choose to defer indefinitely.

It’s possible Healey will surprise us all and announce he is resigning again in protest at his own refusal to meet the 2030 target. But as of today he’s still very much in No 11 and, after some confusion at Wednesday’s prime minister’s questions, the government position is the 2035 deadline.

So Kemi and a few members of her shadow cabinet decamped to the slightly surreal setting of Scotland House London – the inside looks like a greenhouse and is about as sweaty – to tell the country it was 2030 or bust. If we delayed any longer, we would all be dead. If the Russians didn’t kill us, she would. The future of the world depended on her.

Andrew Griffith, Kemi’s new shadow chancellor, made the introductions. You’d have imagined he might be a little embarrassed about his part in writing the Liz Truss mini-budget and his vociferous support for it thereafter, but he isn’t a man much given to self-reflection. Rather, it’s as though he imagines he is doing us all a favour by sharing his brilliance. He started by paying tribute to his predecessor. Poor Mel Stride. Loyal but expendable. Kemi has just revealed her full shadow ministerial team and The Melster is about the only Tory MP not included in Kemi’s new shadow ministerial team.

Then came Kemi. Wake up, peeps, she said. We were as good as at war already. Cyber-attacks. Russian drones on Leipzig airport. A Russian attack on a Nato country nailed on for the next few years. She marvelled at Poland for its 300,000-strong army. That was the kind of country she wanted to lead. She forgot to mention that if she had been prime minister we would probably have been at war earlier this year. She had been all for joining Donald Trump’s war on Iran. It could have been us who killed some women and children at a wedding party this week. What an opportunity missed.

It was all very black and white. If we spent 3% we would all definitely be safe. The Russians and other hostile countries would immediately back off. But a penny less and they would attack for sure. They could spot weakness. So Kemi was preparing for war. She would not shy away from sending men and women to possibly pointless deaths. There would be many more corners of foreign fields that would be forever England.

Just as arbitrary was how this was all to be paid for. It’s almost become axiomatic in rightwing circles that the extra money for defence should be found by cutting the welfare bill. In other words, it’s the poorest and most vulnerable people who will be funding the military. This drew applause from the large audience. All of whom looked as though they were quite comfortably off and would therefore be spared the pain of making any sacrifices themselves. Which is exactly how they like it. That’s what makes them proud to be British.

When it came to the details of where the savings were to be made, Kemi came over all vague. Mumble, mumble. Moving on. Though most of us could have sworn that some of the cuts had already been announced last year and that she was effectively trying to spend the same money twice. But Kemi was adamant that Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, had been all over the details and that nothing had been left to chance. Which wasn’t quite as reassuring as Kemi had hoped.

There was also a commitment to save the money from a Chagos deal that had yet to be agreed and hadn’t even been spent. If I filled in my tax return with such creativity, HMRC would have some questions. But it’s the leader of the opposition and none of this may ever happen so none of this really matters. Kemi ended with a sneer at cheaper bus fares – why can’t people take taxis – and a whole list of taxes she would either abolish or cut. Weirdly, she didn’t think to end the pension triple lock, which most economists think is the only sane thing to do. The audience wouldn’t have been so keen on that.

All this was said with an effortless confidence. Even when she was talking nonsense and contradicting herself. I guess you could call that Kemi’s USP. Her answers to questions about why anyone should bother to listen – when it had been the Tories who had hollowed out the defence budget over the past 14 years – varied from the peace dividend, to everyone had done it, to it had been nothing to do with her and the Conservatives were starting again from scratch. Ground zero does a lot of heavy lifting for Kemi these days.

On one thing she was clear. Are we going to war? asked a reporter from the Express. Hell, yeah, said Kemi. Just watch me. She wouldn’t rest until every child could sleep safe in their bed while missiles were raining down across Britain. It was just a shame that for some kids, those beds might no longer be their own. Kicked out of their homes and forced into insecure accommodation the councils can’t afford. Still, I guess they can get used to a cardboard box. That will teach them to adopt welfare as a lifestyle.

The Bayeux tapestry: a stupefying, thrilling, horrifying masterpiece that shakes the earth

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 14:51:33 GMT

British Museum, LondonThe greatest battle ever depicted in art is here at last – and it hurtles along, making your heart pound with its sense of doom and destiny, culminating in fires and corpses on a battlefield full of pathos

It should not work. It should not even exist. Nothing about the Bayeux tapestry makes sense according to any norms of art: its creators couldn’t do proper portraits or pictorial depth or landscapes or any of the sophisticated things we associate with timeless masterpieces. When they depict a church, they have to write what it is: Ecclesia. But these artists – or who knows, perhaps she was a single artist – created something so stupefying and delightful, so abundant in visual thrills, horrors and humour, it beats almost everything else ever painted or carved – let alone embroidered on a strip of linen.

And now here it is, in front of my eyes, close enough to touch if it wasn’t behind a glass screen of such high quality you never catch a reflection. The British Museum’s display of this wonder is perfect. It’s laid out in its case, the length of a gallery, which you reach after some archaeological foreplay involving armour, quotes from chronicles and info screens. Then you see the colours of the tapestry below you from a parapet – russets, greens, yellows – after which you simply start at the beginning and follow the story rightwards. Surrounded by darkness and picked out by finely adjusted lighting, the Bayeux tapestry shines. My only quibble is the ethereal soundtrack – shouldn’t there be drums, oliphants, troubadours?

I managed a pretty satisfying eyeful in under an hour, although more than the allotted 40 minutes. This is pacy art: it hurtles along. In fact, that’s how it embraces you. Your heart pounds with a sense of doom and destiny. This is, you realise, the greatest battle in art.

It has plenty of competition. Battles and war have engrossed artists down the millennia, from Trajan’s Column to Picasso’s Guernica, usually in scenes of hopeless chaos. So one thing that’s unique about the Bayeux tapestry, and key to its dramatic zip, is the clear and definitive nature of the battle it depicts.

On 14 October 1066, Harold, recently crowned king of Anglo-Saxon England, and his army faced the newly landed forces of William, Duke of Normandy, near Hastings. By the end of the day, Harold was dead, along with devastating numbers of his soldiers and nobles – and the Normans had conquered England. They never left. This battle changed a nation and William succeeded where those later would-be cross-Channel invaders – Philip II of Spain, Napoleon and Hitler – would all fail.

So a big battle with a very clear conclusion. As you pad along the British Museum display, savouring lovely details like a servant eavesdropping on a conversation, or one of Harold’s people carrying his hunting dog to a ship so it doesn’t get its paws wet, you are led through the buildup to the big fight with mounting excitement.

When hell is finally unleashed, the Norman cavalry pound with such force you can almost hear hooves shake the earth. Norman archers fire continuous volleys that send arrow shafts straight into Saxon bodies. Meanwhile, the Saxons stand manfully in hauberks with their axes and take it. They give it, too, to the point that William seems for a moment to be losing the day, horses tipping over, knights falling.

It’s in such images that the Bayeux tapestry transcends everything you could reasonably expect of a medieval artwork. The scene where the Norman cavalry seems to falter is simultaneously realistic and nightmarish. One horse is completely upended, its face to the earth, rear legs in the sky. Another tips over as its rider slides forward, his armoured body suddenly a helpless rag.

As you move along the strip, what hits you is its brilliant sense of momentum. Early on, two messengers race across the French countryside, their hair flying out behind them in straight black threads: it’s a thrilling way to convey speed. Such bone-shaking velocity is shown again and again in superbly simple ways. At Hastings, you see the Norman knights gradually gather pace. Their horses calmly prance, riders bolt upright with lances aloft, then one rider tilts forward as his horse lowers its head and bends its front legs in a run. Soon the legs of all the horses are flying in rhythm as the knights hold their lances ready to throw, adding to the sense of forward thrust.

It’s the 11th-century answer to Eadweard Muybridge’s motion photograph sequences. We follow the change in speed as if it was happening to a single figure. The Normans are so disciplined they seem be to one single, lethal horseman – and that is why they will win.

While you are dragged forward, you are also led up and down, to meander in a marginal world of monsters and myths. Bizarre goings-on in the borders above and below the action constantly interrupt the drive of the story. The gryphons, dragons and square-winged, hieratic birds of prey seem much bigger and bolder in life than reproduction and harder to ignore.

I thought I’d detected some structure to it all: the top margin is more ordered and sublime, suggesting the heavenly sphere (Halley’s Comet speeds through it like a rocket), while the creatures below look earthy and sinful. Then I saw two bare-chested female centaurs at the top spreading their arms out as if to say: “Lo and behold!” So much for logic.

The great thing about a border is that you can break it. When William’s ships speed across the Channel, their bulging, wind-filled, multicoloured sails fill the upper space. As the Battle of Hastings gets bloodier, bodies and body parts pile up in the lower one.

In both the borders and central strip, the Bayeux tapestry always set its action in a wider world, and even, when it shows the comet, a larger cosmos. As the armoured elite go to war, peasants plough and sow the fields. They are portrayed in distracting, vibrant detail and this workaday scene as the battle approaches is pointed and poignant: whoever wins, whoever rules England, country people will still work the soil. That same sudden cutaway from the rulers’ perspective happens when a woman and her child watch the Normans set their house on fire. But what you can see here, close to the stitches in such good light, is that one of the men torching the house also seems sad and conflicted.

It’s that honesty that makes this not just a fascinating medieval relic but a universal depiction of the madness that is war. If the violence is stunningly real, so are its consequences. The dead bodies pile up in mounds as Saxon after Saxon falls. King Harold didn’t really get killed by an arrow in his eye we are told, but seeing the tapestry so close, it sure looks like it. Anyway, his royal body just joins the rest. In the final scenes, the peasants, the churls, get their revenge. Little shabby figures pull the mailed hauberks off dead knights, leaving them naked.

It’s a final flourish of the precocious artistic brilliance of these 11th-century artists and craftspeople. Naked bodies emerge from their armour, pale and oddly beautiful – the complete ones, at least – as these medieval geniuses show they can depict, through embroidery, incredibly gentle, intimate nudes whose dead flesh fills the battlefield with pathos.

It ends there. But, although there’s a lost later section, this anticlimax looks perfect to me. By then, I had been drained by this epic in all its tragedy and comedy. Bodies and body parts. That’s where the war talk was heading all along.

At the British Museum, London, 10 September-11 July

Iran targets US bases as Israel warns sanctions could drive Tehran to ‘desperate steps’

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 14:16:54 GMT

Air bases used by US in UAE and Kuwait hit as Israeli defence chief says Iran’s regime fears collapse due to economic pressures

Iran has continued to demonstrate an ability to target bases in the Gulf used by the US despite six months of war and a new sanctions regime described by the Trump administration as an “economic D-day”.

As Iran’s military targeted US bases in the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait, despite threats of further strikes by the US president, Israel’s defence chief warned that economic pressures from the sanctions could lead Tehran to escalate to more “extreme measures”.

“This morning, the army hit the satellite communication systems, equipment depots and fighter aircraft hangars of the terrorist US army at the Ahmad al-Jaber air base in Kuwait with missiles and drones,” the Iranian military said on Thursday in a statement carried by state television.

The “location of forces and radar systems of the child-killing US army at the Al Minhad air base in the UAE were also attacked by missiles and drones of the army”, it added.

In a post on X, Kuwait’s ministry of defence said its air defences had intercepted missile and drone attacks during a “blatant Iranian aggression”.

The Kuwaiti statement came after the US allies Bahrain and Jordan said their air defence systems intercepted several Iranian air attacks on Wednesday.

Fighting between the US and Iran has increased this week after the US hit Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz on Sunday, claiming that Iran was planning to use them to shoot mines into the waterway.

The latest flare-up in the conflict comes amid little evidence that the Trump administration is succeeding in advancing its nebulous war aims either on the battlefield or via mediation, despite the US president’s repeated claims to have opened the strait of Hormuz to oil traffic.

Instead, traffic through the key maritime passageway remains far below prewar levels, with oil prices remaining stubbornly elevated ahead of US midterm elections. Oil prices jumped again on Thursday after the Iranian strikes.

Among the weapons Iran has used this week is its Kheibar Shekan medium-range ballistic missile system. The cheap and accurate missile can be launched within minutes and has become a staple of Iranian strikes.

The rocket’s solid fuel motor means it does not require lengthy fuelling. It can be deployed very quickly to avoid detection and can be armed with a powered and steerable final stage to help beat anti-missile systems.

Despite claims by the Trump administration that Tehran is running out of rockets, Iran continues to fire missiles that are considerably cheaper to produce than the US interceptors used to shoot them down.

Iran has claimed as recently as the end of August that it maintained both missiles stockpiles and the ability to manufacture them.

“Initially, some believed that Iran had only a limited number of missiles and that its stockpiles would eventually be depleted as the war continued,” the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson Brig Gen Hossein Mohebbi said.

“However, that assumption proved incorrect, as Iran’s missile capability has remained sustained and its missile production has continued.” Mohebbi’s characterisation of Iranian missile stockpiles could not be verified.

The continued strikes came as Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, said that while the new US economic sanctions appeared to be effective, the increased pressure could lead Tehran into extreme measures.

“We see signs indicating that the heavy economic pressure they are under, and the fear of an uprising and the collapse of the regime, may push them to desperate steps,” Katz said at a ceremony for defence ministry employees.

The hawkish minister reiterated the threats against the Islamic Republic that he has made in recent months.

“An Iranian attack on Israel will free Israel from any existing constraint,” he said. “We will strike all of Iran’s national military and civilian infrastructure – including energy infrastructure – and push Iran deep back into the stone age.”

An Unexpected Life by Gloria Steinem review – a fitting tribute to a feminist icon

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 14:16:33 GMT

The activist’s memoir, due to be published this month, now stands as a posthumous testament to her remarkable life

Gloria Steinem was due to speak at a women’s lunch in New York at the end of this month and at more events in October, illustrating the central theme of An Unexpected Life, her new memoir, which, when it’s published a few weeks from now, will stand as posthumous testament to the 92-year-old icon: just keep going. So it is, after her death on Wednesday, that the book’s opening pages unfold with a deep, added poignancy and when Steinem expresses gratitude for a life that has been both happier and longer “than I ever imagined”, one is struck by the greater gratitude we probably owe her.

An Unexpected Life is a follow-up of sorts to My Life on the Road, the activist’s memoir of a decade ago, and as the tributes pour in, the book offers us an opportunity to go back over Steinem’s hardscrabble origins in Toledo, Ohio, and the roots of her activism. This is where it all happened, the formation of a woman who would come to define second wave feminism by combining a tough-as-they-come stance with something that looked a lot like serenity. Reading the first half of the book, one is reminded of Steinem’s original power and the improbability and iconoclasm of her journey, in which a childhood governed by poverty and dysfunction turned into a lifelong mission to resist the narrow templates laid out for her.

It’s a cracking backstory. Steinem’s rackety father was a travelling salesman of sorts, touring the country with a dance pavilion that saw Steinem spend long stretches of her childhood with him on the road, which, she writes, conditioned her to enjoy a similarly unconventional existence in adulthood. When she was at home, the young Steinem was a carer for her increasingly mentally unwell mother, who was frequently to be found wandering the town in her nightdress, and Steinem writes movingly about what it is to grow up ashamed of your house and your family. “I learned I could survive almost anything,” she writes, “including a sad mother who was called the Crazy Lady of the neighborhood. We are all one human family, and we are responsible for one another.”

Raised on instability, Steinem grew up remarkably free of the pressure weighing on most of her female peers to knuckle down into conventional marriage and motherhood, leaving her free to pursue a life as a freelance writer and, later, an activist. After college, she went to India for two years, a defining period that informed her outlook to the very end, and on return, began her career as a campaigning journalist, which culminated in her co-founding of Ms magazine in 1971 and eventual ascent to the head of the women’s movement.

These periods of her life are well documented. What I found interesting in the book were Steinem’s asides about the cost of pursuing the life she chose. “Though I managed to support myself,” she writes, “I didn’t save money until I was past fifty. I was sure that I’d end up as a bag lady, like women I saw sleeping in subway stations. I used to handle that fear by thinking, It’s a life like any other. I’ll organize the other bag ladies.” She eventually became somewhat financially secure, largely thanks to buying part of a 19th-century brownstone on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, the beloved home in which she died this week – although a throwaway line towards the end of the book suggests she was still paying off her mortgage well into her 80s, an astonishing fact given her fame.

Steinem is the real thing, of course; she was never in it for the money. She makes a strong case that she wasn’t in it for the attention, either, although, as a talented speaker and organiser, she drew on great reserves of magnetism that over the years caused her a lot of problems with jealousy from within the movement, and condescension from without. Right until the end, Steinem was stewarding large groups of women – famous and otherwise – at “talking circles” in her house and putting herself at the centre of a conversation she had in some ways begun.

A big strand of these debates was the shoe-horning of women into flat, unfulfilled lives, which they are conditioned to believe are the only desirable option. This is where the book’s startling honesty comes into play, a habit Steinem seems to have had from the get-go. Some years after graduating, she wrote to her Smith College classmates in an alumni newsletter: “I’m quite broke, not at all who I thought I would be – and consciously happy.”

She writes powerfully about women who made different, unhappier choices under pain of social death: “I remember one woman, married to a socially acceptable man much older than she, who explained, ‘After he dies, I’ll be free.’ The cost of freedom seemed to mean she was able to live only in the future.” It is useful to be reminded of how bad things were so very recently. As the book informs us, “in the 1960s Columbia Law School had a 5% quota for women” – in an era in which American women were earning, on average, 59 cents on each dollar earned by men. (“Now,” she writes, “they typically earn 82 cents for every dollar earned by men. At the going rate, it will be fifty years before we reach parity overall, and seventy-five years for African American women to reach parity with African American men.”)

There are glowing, drive-by sketches of some of the famous figures Steinem encountered on the road, including James Baldwin and Annie Leibovitz. She is disinclined to offer anything but praise for the people she admires and so the book’s only waspish assessment is reserved for Andy Warhol, whose smirking sensibility really flies up Steinem’s nose and sits poorly alongside her earnestness. I like her for this – having a crack at the immensely irritating Warhol, about whom, she sniffs, “It seems a low point of the art world that Andy Warhol’s is considered valuable.”

As we enter the post-Steinem era – a statement that seems outlandish, given the length and ardour of her service – it’s a pleasure, simply, to spend time in her company, and her role as an elder is one she takes seriously, evoking her deep relationship with Native Americans as the basis for many of her insights. “The patriarchal nuclear family, the one that we are supposed to think is the only kind of family, is really only about 150 years old, and almost entirely a function of industrialization and capitalism.”

Sign up to Bookmarks

after newsletter promotion

It wasn’t until she was much older, she writes, that she realised so much of her life “was spent doing what was expected of me, and not enough doing what I loved”. Counterintuitively, this included her hard line on marriage, which she set herself against as a matter of principle, only marrying her great love, David Bale, at 66 and staying with him until he died three years later. This is the old Steinem we love, the combination of absolute force and, hard on its heels, admission of error.

After all the doubt and indecision, Steinem at 92 had a very clear idea of what she was supposed to be doing, and my God she did it right to the end. “My role as an older person is to remind us how far we have come, and with age comes the responsibility to keep learning. As Robert Browning wrote: ‘The best is yet to be, / The last of life, / for which the first was made.’” Or as Steinem put it, with a hard-won smile it’s impossible to resist, “Now even my jeans are much older than many people I work with.” We should all be so lucky; what a life.

An Unexpected Life by Gloria Steinem is published by Ebury in the UK and Random House in the US. To support the Guardian buy a copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

‘I have an obsession with barber shops’: kd lang on her prairies upbringing, Patsy Cline and being shaved by Cindy Crawford

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 14:00:39 GMT

The Canadian singer-songwriter answers your questions about her trailblazing career, her spirituality, and collaborations with the likes of Neko Case, Laura Veirs and Pee-wee Herman

I left the Canadian prairies many years ago, but they remain my home. How do you feel about that part of western Canada, where the prairies meet the Rocky mountains, which shaped us both? What does Alberta mean to you now? NicholasLittleAll of my artistic preferences were formed by the minimalism of the prairies, by the affordable space and the stillness. There weren’t many things around, so a field with bales would be this incredibly graphic moment, or a tree or a certain hill – very small increments of beauty placed in vast amounts of space. The sky was very important and a feeling of – I wouldn’t say loneliness, but solace, perhaps. That’s my bottom line, my basic instinct. It’s the frame that that informs all of my art, the way I decorate my house, the way I sing, the way I dress. That sort of minimalist nature is embedded in me.

Many people can sing a song well, but you’re a vocalist who emotes raw vulnerability. Do you work like a method actor – entering, or reliving, the reality of the song during the practice period? verdantearthI try to sink myself into the lyrics for sure. I try to create visuals, sort of an emotional internal movie of what the lyrics possess, to relive it emotionally. With [Case/Lang/Veirs track] Honey and Smoke, for example, I imagine watching somebody I’m in love with dancing with somebody else and feeling jealousy.

How proud are you of that infamous Vanity Fair cover shoot [in which Cindy Crawford “shaves” kd in a barber’s chair]? Trumansdad

Very. I was friends with Herb [Ritts] and somehow I got the opportunity to do the Vanity Fair cover, and he was shooting it. I was obsessed with a French movie called The Hairdresser’s Husband at the time. I have kind of an obsession with cutting hair and barber shops. I don’t know where that came from – actually, I just realised why, and I’ve never told anyone this! My dad’s drugstore in the really small town I grew up in – the next business over was a barber shop, so I used to watch the barber cutting hair all the time. It must be some sort of childhood visualisation imprint or something. I suggested to Herb, maybe we can do it in a barber’s chair. He phoned me a few days later and said, “I have Cindy Crawford.” I was like, “OK!” We shot it on the roof of his building in downtown Hollywood, up on the roof at golden hour. It was magical. Cindy was super professional, as you can imagine. She’s a model, so it was her realm. I was trying to behave and not be an idiot. It was incredible, and I knew that it had a certain gravity to it. After all these years, I feel like we made a piece of art and a significant social statement, and I really have such pride about it.

LS: You have a very cheeky look on your face on the cover. Yeah. I mean, come on!

Could you name some of your favourite visual artists and explain why you love them? Do you own art? SimotherI can’t afford to be a collector, but I’m certainly a fan. I love everything; some of my favourite painters are Franz Kline, because I love the confidence with which he painted, and Agnes Martin because I love patterns and simplicity. She’s also from Alberta. I really gravitate towards abstract expressionism just because I love that the emotion is driving it. That’s how I relate to art, emotionally rather than intellectually.

Looking back 10 years on, what do you remember most about Case/Lang/Veirs? And would you be tempted to work with Neko Case and Laura Veirs again if the stars aligned? VerulamiumParkRangerI remember how excited I was when I had the idea to collaborate with them. When I texted them, they both answered within half an hour. And then the work began. I remember it being quite difficult in terms of having three major artists, who had been bosses their whole lives, coming together – we had to navigate and reformulate how we worked, the structure of writing and creativity. They’re both incredible songwriters. I’m in awe of their songwriting ability, and I had to stay out of the way because I felt like they were so much more prolific than I was. We ended up being real good friends, and we had an exciting but short tour.

What was it like being part of the Vancouver music scene and performing at the Railway Club in the 80s? budthespudYou must be a Canadian. The Railway Club and the Savoy Club in Vancouver were extremely important to my career. They were both really great small alternative independent music venues. The person who booked the music, Janet Forsyth, booked me very early, and the buzz started happening. It was an incredibly vibrant and buzzy time for me. The shows were extremely formative because I was trying out a lot of different material, learning how to be a stage performer. To this day, Janet Forsyth is my best friend.

What was it like to be a part of the Pee-wee’s Playhouse Christmas Special (AKA the greatest, gayest Christmas special ever made)? My little brother and I have watched it together every year since 1988! AlexisHidellIt was amazing – it was magical because it was so unbridled. I just sang a Christmas carol – it was all carols, but he had really contrasting artists like Grace Jones and Doris Day. It was like he had all these different kites and he was flying them all at once. You could do whatever you wanted and it was joyful and wise and sardonic – it contained everything. It’s not unlike the paintings we were talking about: it’s emotional expression without any constraints, artistic freedom. Paul [Reubens, AKA Pee-wee Herman] and I became friends. I loved the documentary Matt Wolf made on him. Paul was serious and very deliberate.

Would you ever consider a follow-up to [lang’s 2004 album of cover versions] Hymns of the 49th Parallel? Hearing Canadian music treated with that kind of deep respect and understanding – the individual songs and the way they exist in conversation with each other – changed something for a lot of people, I think. MarnaNightingaleI have been asked that by my record company and my manager, but I really try to honour my muse and my instincts. It hasn’t happened yet, but maybe it will. Certainly the material is there. There’s an embarrassment of riches of great Canadian songwriting.

What was it like appearing on the Larry Sanders show? CaptainLibIt was fun. He was a beautiful guy. [The show was] an intense niche to be put into because they have their own vernacular and rhythm and way of being. I tried to inhabit my own space with it and be natural, but man, the energy there was kind of like being placed in the middle of a football game, and somebody’s vacuuming naked … I don’t totally remember what happened.

You’ve described your connection with Patsy Cline as “otherworldly”. What is it about her – and the emotional landscapes of songs such as Leavin’ on Your Mind – that gives her such enduring appeal? Bopalena_now_JohnnyThe emotional connection is inexplicable. Emotion is something ethereal and indescribable. Patsy contained an empathy, an earthiness, a vulnerability, a sense of humour – all the essential parts of humanity. She just sang from an open place, and let people feel comfortable immersing themselves in her.

The accordion is prominent not just in the beautiful Constant Craving but in multiple other recordings of yours. Can you tell us more about your accordionist, Teddy Borowiecki, and do you have a particular fascination with this instrument? BirtyDankersIt was around in my upbringing because in the Canadian prairies there were a lot of German and Polish eastern Europeans who had migrated to Canada, so it was prevalent in dance bands and so forth. And Teddy, who is Polish, was a very good accordion player, so I wanted to utilise his talent.

What can you share about your meditation practice, and how it has affected you, the living of your life, and your music? SillyputtyMy spiritual practice is inseparable from anything I do, and is of utmost importance. It’s taken precedence over all things in my life. So I don’t even know where to start or how to describe it. It’s given me a different point of reference that has anchored me in motivation and purpose. Just taking my contribution to the universe very seriously – not self-righteously, but the desire to be authentic and uncontrived.

The 10th anniversary edition of Case/Lang/Veirs is released via Anti- on 4 September
