I own six guns. Here’s how to talk to conservatives about firearms

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 13:30:39 GMT

In rural America, guns are a fact of life. But even conservatives agree that properly locking them up is crucial in preventing deaths

I have six guns in my house.

The first was a vintage Winchester 12-gauge. It was the winter of 1990, and my husband and I had just moved from an urban block in north-west Philadelphia to a 100-year-old farmhouse in Appalachian Virginia, where my family goes back seven generations.

That spring, we started sitting out back every night with the two outdoor dogs and 13 feral barn cats we had adopted since moving in. Invariably, our new neighbor Jimmy would drive by and stop for a beer.

One evening in March, the three of us looked up to see a bat flying out of the old attic. Then another, and another. We stopped counting at 100. Since our only access to the attic was through a 2ft hole in the closet ceiling, we installed a door in the hallway with a drop-down ladder.

After clearing out countless piles of hidden guano, we began to worry about histoplasmosis – not to mention rabies – as the vexatious critters clawed at the edges of the new entrance, trying to squeeze their way into the house. By mid-summer, we still had not succeeded in humanely relocating what was clearly a firmly established colony.

In exasperation, we turned to our newfound repository of rural knowledge – Jimmy – who brought over his old shotgun and suggested we shoot in the air to scare them away. The bats made an immediate 180 and proceeded to chase after the shot, as if they were tracking down moths and mosquitoes.

We lost no bats, but we did gain a gun.

Our second came the next fall. As with many rural homesteads, when the Department of Transportation straightened out the road decades earlier, they located it 20ft from our front porch. My husband was out of town a good bit that summer, and someone set up a ratty old trailer at one end of our two-mile, gravel road. An abandoned farmhouse sat at the other end, and a group of single male squatters moved in.

Foot traffic grew between the two, and we suspected meth was changing hands. While I was alone one night, a particularly rough-looking fellow from the trailer stumbled up the front steps to “borrow the phone”. That weekend we took a trip to Walmart and added a 20-gauge Remington youth model to our collection.

When my mom died 10 years later, I inherited her old BB gun and Remington 22; my husband also inherited one of each. He says the two childhood BB guns don’t really count, but I think they do.

When I told a second amendment-supporting friend about our collection, she said: “You need to lock them up or get rid of them.”

I don’t disagree.

In rural America, guns are a fact of life. But the preventable deaths that come with unsecured firearms don’t have to be.

That is why, for the past two years, I’ve been working with liberal volunteers to find common ground with conservative gun owners, beginning with something remarkably simple: giving away gun locks.

As national director of Community Works, a program of the Rural Urban Bridge Initiative, I bring together volunteers across political differences to address practical needs in their home communities.

Progressives won’t gain traction in rural areas by showing up at election time and asking people to change their politics. We have to earn trust year-round by acting locally alongside our conservative neighbors to make things better for everyone: cleaning up rivers, repairing homes, distributing food – even saving lives.

When working shoulder-to-shoulder with fellow volunteers one day, it’s harder to turn around and demonize them the next. National depictions of Democrats as godless baby-killers or Republicans as gun-waving racists just don’t hold up when those same folks are standing next to you handing out diapers and school supplies, or packing food for students in the free-lunch program.

Promoting gun safety put that concept to an unusually difficult test. Guns, after all, are one of the subjects widely considered unbridgeable in rural politics.

I was aware of that when I asked volunteers to hand out free gun locks in some of Virginia’s most conservative counties. I also knew the stakes: firearms are the leading cause of death among American children and teenagers, killing 2,581 children under 18 in 2023 alone.

But decades of polarization have made it near impossible to agree on even the simplest measures. Liberals caricature gun owners as uneducated rednecks or reckless young men stockpiling AR-15s; gun owners see liberals as bleeding hearts determined to confiscate their weapons. But keeping guns away from children seemed like the one place where we might meet.

The Gun Aware Project (Gap) was founded by Karen and Nick Fischer after a local high school murder-suicide in 2023. Gap organizes free gun-lock distributions during fall back-to-school events in public schools, and volunteers from Community Works were eager to help.

One of the first distributions took place in Giles county, on the West Virginia border. There, a growing number of residents support seceding from Virginia and joining West Virginia, in part because they believe Virginia’s new gun laws threaten their second amendment rights.

It would be easy to dismiss such a group with the “ignorant hillbilly” stereotype, except for the fact that my physical therapist and her doctor husband were thinking about joining. Despite the gun lobby’s success in pitting gun owners against those who aren’t – always leading to bigger gun sales – the “sides” are often more fluid than we’ve been led to believe.

Maybe that’s why the Giles county sheriff’s office, a strong defender of second amendment rights, agreed to collaborate with the Gun Aware Project. Sheriff W Morgan Millirons issued a statement describing firearm safety as part of responsible gun ownership.

To date, Gap has given away more than 4,000 locks, 1,000 of those to local departments like Millirons’. Volunteers have spoken with more than 15,000 people in a four-county area. No proselytizing – just sharing storage safety information along with the locks.

The Fischers say they have been surprised by the number of people in NRA hats and camo who say: “I really like what you’re doing, we need to protect our kids.” The second most common response is more what they expected: “I have a right to have a weapon. Why are you people trying to take it away?”

Attuned to the rural gun culture in which they are operating, the Fischers acknowledge the second amendment, and then redirect the conversation back to safety.

Karen explains that removing the magazine from a semi-automatic firearm does not necessarily unload it: a live round may remain in the chamber, something most children – and even some gun owners – do not realize. After listening to Karen, and learning the locks were free, one woman asked for enough locks to secure 12 guns, saying it would be a Christmas gift to her husband.

“The issue is not about taking away the second amendment,” says Nick. “The issue is how we deal with living with the second amendment.”

In the same vein, the goal of Community Works is not to overcome, or try to change, rural culture. It’s about understanding, respecting and learning to live alongside our conservative rural neighbors.

Early research suggests the approach may be working. More than 4,400 surveys were conducted before and after the launch of Community Works in six pilot counties in Virginia and Georgia, along with nearby counties without the new program.

According to the study’s author, the Colby College social scientist Dr Nicholas Jacobs, residents in participating counties became less influenced by national partisan divisions and more likely to judge parties by how well they governed locally. They began to view local Democrats as distinct from national party stereotypes, instead judging people based on their contributions to the community.

What we did not foresee is that Community Works would also change the way rural Democrats viewed and interacted with their communities.

One Democratic volunteer who helped to hand out gun locks at a rural high school event reflected: “I was actually kind of scared to do this in gun country. I thought they’d call me ‘woke’ and walk right on by. But all the kids and parents were really nice, and they totally agreed with me about gun safety.”

Her apprehension was understandable. For generations, rural people – and particularly Appalachians with guns – have been portrayed as violent and backward. If you’ve seen the 1972 movie Deliverance or the more recent Netflix series Justified, you know what I’m talking about.

Historically, the Appalachian hillbilly stereotype was created in the late 1800s by “local color” travel writers to sell their stories to urban readers. Shotguns, moonshine, bad teeth and dirty overalls were all part of the image. The timber, coal and railroad industries soon adopted the negative caricature as justification for their abusive exploitation of Appalachian landowners.

It worked. By successfully casting their victims as ignorant, uncivilized and dangerous – as “other” – the corporate profiteers were given societal sanction to deceitfully extract natural resources that then reaped them huge returns in urban centers.

Since then, urban and suburban liberals have been told over and over again to be wary of folks born and raised “country”, especially those with guns.

Such was the case when White Rural Rage: The Threat to American Democracy, was released in 2024. With captions proclaiming “[w]hite rural voters are the most dangerous and anti-democratic group in the United States,” the authors promoted the more sensational aspects of their research on numerous morning talkshows.

In one 40-second soundbite, they accused white rural voters of being racist, xenophobic, anti-immigrant and anti-gay, leading to their conclusion that white rural rage was the greatest threat to American democracy. At the time, the city-based authors received a good deal of backlash from Appalachian and rural advocates for their use of tropes and stereotypes to sell their book.

I often use my son’s friends as a barometer for gauging declarations I read about conservative rural white folks, especially young white males. Born and raised here, my son’s a country boy just like his friends, but unlike him, they were raised in families that have voted Republican for decades. Not even FDR or JFK were able to carry the vote in our county. Kids here wear camo and seed caps, drive pickup trucks, and skip school the first day of hunting season. They are also some of the nicest, most respectful, young people I know.

From where I stand, the idea of white rural rage as the driving force behind the downfall of democracy is just one more example of the perpetuation of stereotypes that divide the rural working class from our counterparts and natural allies in the cities.

Now, instead of the timber, coal and railroad barons benefiting, we have tech and software billionaires and corporate giants, including gun manufacturers, who wield massive control over information and commerce.

And just as in the late 19th century, it’s to the advantage of these new titans to keep the rest of us separated and blaming each other for school shootings and the price of gas and groceries, as in, “you got what you voted for.”

I’d like to think we’ve learned something in 150 years: that by working together across lines of geography, race, class, party and even guns, we might build a more equitable future.

For myself, after handing out scores of gun locks to my neighbors, I’ll be donating half our guns to a local effort called Groceries Not Guns, and safely storing the others using my brand new locks.

Meredith Dean is the national director of the Rural Urban Bridge Initiative’s Community Works program. Previously, she served as chair of her local Democratic party, field director for a congressional campaign, and was the founding director of a non-profit dedicated to empowering Appalachian women to actively engage in democracy

The Ceuta border breach was leapt on by Europe’s right. That doesn’t absolve Spain

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 13:29:48 GMT

The government’s sluggish response has been disastrous for everyone involved – and for Sánchez’s message on immigration

More than a month after an estimated 72,000 people suddenly crossed from Morocco into the Spanish territory of Ceuta, the city remains in chaos and the damage inflicted on the Spanish government is becoming clearer. Most of those who made the crossing have returned to Morocco. The scale of the incident was nevertheless extraordinary, and about 140 people are thought to have died.

Also extraordinary was the response of the 22 EU governments that rounded on the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, rather than demonstrate the solidarity one might expect from allies. Perhaps less surprising was the exploitation of the crisis by rightwing and far-right parties in Spain and beyond, Donald Trump’s attacks and the interventions of Russian state-linked actors and Israeli critics on social media to fuel division.

But this opportunism by Europe’s rightwing governments – Italy suspended its Schengen arrangements with Spain for no good reason – does not absolve Spain of blame. What has unfolded since 30 July is tragic for Ceuta, which has a permanent population of only about 84,000 people, and for the thousands of people, including an estimated 1,200 unaccompanied children, left on its streets and beaches. Sánchez’s government must take responsibility for some of the damage it is now belatedly trying to mop up.

On 1 August, in the aftermath of the border breach, Sánchez reassured the EU that “virtually all” of the people who had arrived in Ceuta had returned to Morocco. The overwhelming majority did indeed leave, but thousands did not – and they are still in the city. Official numbers have fluctuated. The Spanish government’s estimate is that 5,000 of those who arrived are still in Ceuta; the region’s local government has suggested it could be double that. For weeks, there was no accommodation available, and hundreds are still camped on beaches or near the overcrowded migrant centres.

People living near these centres complain they cannot leave their apartments out of fear, and that their children are unable to play on the beach or in the street. Businesses have had to close for days on end, incurring losses. Summer festivities had to be cancelled. Many migrants, including women and children, have survived on charity from local NGOs, the Red Cross and neighbours, and have little food, water and shelter.

Yet as the situation deteriorated, the Spanish government failed for weeks to appoint anyone to coordinate a response. This would have been essential in Spain’s decentralised system, with powers divided between the central government and local and regional authorities. Now Madrid is finally funnelling resources and money into the matter, but only after the situation had deteriorated dangerously.

Tensions have been evident in recent days, with local people crying in front of TV cameras, and politicians pleading for help. Protests directed against migrants have been constant. They have been mostly peaceful, but there have been outbreaks of violence. In one incident, a group of protesters tried to drive migrants off the beach and burned their tents before they were dispersed by the police with teargas. In another, military police were allegedly assaulted by a group from Morocco. At least 23 sexual assaults against migrants have been reported, including nine against children.

Ceuta was already fragile. The city, smaller than the site of Madrid airport, is home to a multicultural community that has been part of Spain since the 17th century. But even before this, its citizens complained about feeling abandoned. And now Morocco is reviving claims of sovereignty.

Sánchez’s defence of Morocco – telling parliament on Thursday that there was “no evidence” that Rabat had orchestrated events at the border – is at odds with popular sentiment in Ceuta and with most of the parties in parliament, including his leftwing allies Sumar, the minority partner in the governing coalition.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

The Spanish government’s slow response and state of denial are damaging not only for Ceuta, but for Madrid’s own message on immigration. Spain has quite successfully promoted immigration as a force for good in recent years, even as most governments in Europe have moved in the opposite direction. What happened in Ceuta should not diminish the case for immigration as a factor driving economic growth and social dynamism, as Spain has shown over the past decade. But the mismanagement of Ceuta on the ground will inevitably impair that message.

Even now, the Spanish government is backtracking, tightening its migration rules and pointing to disinformation around a supreme court decision that protected migrants’ rights against speedy returns as a cause for the rush on Ceuta. It has said it will stop transferring unaccompanied minors out of the territory and distributing them around the country for their protection, and is approving restrictions in line with the hardline EU pact on migration and asylum pushed by rightwing governments.

Regional politicians, who are mostly conservative, refuse to help out. The conservative People’s party (PP), which is leading in the polls before next year’s general election, is always better at attacking the government than clarifying what it would do differently. But even some local politicians from the Socialist Workers’ party have recently joined demonstrations in solidarity with Ceuta.

The Ceuta episode has landed Spain with an almost impossible situation to resolve. But a combination of passivity and blaming everyone but Morocco has not helpedthe city’s residents, Sánchez’s political position or the positive case for immigration in Spain and beyond.

María Ramírez is a journalist and deputy managing editor of elDiario. es, a news outlet in Spain

‘We badly need to raise our boys more like our girls’: Gloria Steinem – a life in quotes

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 13:07:32 GMT

The groundbreaking feminist and acclaimed writer has died aged 92 and leaves behind her a wealth of wit and wisdom

Gloria Steinem, groundbreaking feminist campaigner, dies aged 92

Hillary Clinton leads tributes to Gloria Steinem: ‘Her activism was rooted in optimism’

Gloria Steinem, the boundary-pushing campaigner and author who spent her life fighting for greater rights for women, has died at the age of 92.

Throughout her career, she was known for her unfiltered honesty and from the 1960s forward, used her words to inspire and bring together women who also wanted to see a change in their lives.

Here are some of her greatest quotes:

“Don’t think about making women fit the world‬ – ‪think about making the world fit women.”‬

“It’s alarming to me that women are still encouraged to blame themselves. No one can do it all.”

“Women have always been an equal part of the past. We just haven’t been a part of history.”‬

“Women may be the one group that grows more radical with age.”

“Feminism has never been about getting a job for one woman. It’s about making life more fair for women everywhere. It’s not about a piece of the existing pie; there are too many of us for that. It’s about baking a new pie.”

“A liberated woman is one who has sex before marriage and a job after.”

“Men should think twice before making widowhood woman’s only path to power.”

“We badly need to raise our boys more like our girls.”

“We’ll never solve the feminization of power until we solve the masculinity of wealth.”

“I always tell younger women: ‘Don’t worry, eventually all your old lovers will be your friends.’”

“If women are supposed to be less rational and more emotional at the beginning of our menstrual cycle when the female hormone is at its lowest level, then why isn’t it logical to say that, in those few days, women behave the most like the way men behave all month long?”‬

“I have yet to hear a man ask for advice on how to combine marriage and a career.”

“[Abortion] is supposed to make us a bad person. But I must say, I never felt that. I used to sit and try and figure out how old the child would be, trying to make myself feel guilty. But I never could!”

“Every economics course ought to start not with production but with reproduction. It is way more important.”

“Listen, honey, if men could get pregnant, abortion would be a sacrament.”

“Patriarchy – or whatever you want to call it, the systems that say there’s masculine and feminine and other bullshit – is about controlling reproduction.”

“Politics is just unequal power. Who does the dishes is political. In the politics of commerciality, if you want to put it that way, the way women’s bodies are looked at, we’re supposed to be ornaments not instruments.”

“I never wanted to be a politician or elected person myself, so I loved to work for other women who did – and hope that more girls will do that. The problem is the feeling that we’re divided from politics, that our vote doesn’t count or what we do doesn’t count. In fact, everything we do counts.”

“They won’t take us seriously. We’re just talking wombs.”

“If you’re a woman, all they can think about your relationship with a politician is that you’re either sleeping with him or advising him about clothes.”

“We are the women our parents warned us against, and we are proud.”

“I wasn’t going to let things happen to me. I was going to direct my life.”

“After feminism, I suddenly realized: not everyone has to live the same way.”

“Either I am invisible, or someone I identify with is invisible, and it makes me so angry.”

“Writing is the only thing that when I do it, I don’t feel I should be doing something else.”

“The art of life is not controlling what happens to us, but using what happens to us.”‬

“Honesty about our age would help. I always try to say my age because I figure it’s a form of coming out.”

“I’m skeptical, but optimistic. I’m not pessimistic because I think pessimism defeats you before you start. I’m skeptical because it’s important to be realistic and use our energies well, but hope is a form of planning.”

Fun, flirty and fried to perfection: farewell to Chicken Shop Date, the YouTube show that helped kill off TV

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 12:42:49 GMT

Amelia Dimoldenberg’s series helped turn YouTube into a world-beating phenomenon. As it bows out, we remember its best bits – from mocking MC Ghetts to that sizzling tension with Billie Eilish and Andrew Garfield

When Amelia Dimoldenberg posted a video to social media this week, telling an unknown companion “we need to talk”, it felt like a monumental announcement was on the horizon. And so it came to pass. Chicken Shop Date, Dimoldenberg’s YouTube series, is coming to an end.

The press release covering the announcement came packed with superlatives. Chicken Shop Date has generated 34m hours of views over the years, and has reached 97% of all countries on the planet. What it didn’t mention is that Chicken Shop Date helped to legitimise YouTube as a platform that has taken on – and perhaps beaten – television. The very fact that the Guardian is covering the end of a YouTube video series in the first place is, in part, down to Chicken Shop Date.

Nevertheless, the writing has clearly been on the wall for some time. Dimoldenberg is moving on to bigger and better things – she hosts red carpet interviews for several major awards and is writing a romcom film, plus a YA show for the BBC – but Chicken Shop Date has also started to ossify. What began as a fun and flirty interview show, which thrived on the genuine tension that sometimes occurred between host and guest, has gradually become just another stop on the promotional cycle. It’s hard to try to flirt with someone who has quite clearly just been shoved in front of you by a publicist, as has been the case in some recent episodes (Ben Stiller, Elmo).

Still, it’s easy to see why the show was so popular. Dimoldenberg’s entire demeanour, simultaneously needy and passive aggressive, has made for compelling viewing over the years. In terms of sheer pop culture heft, it’s worth remembering that it was Dimoldenberg who first goaded Louis Theroux into reprising a rap he first performed in a documentary 26 years ago. It immediately went viral. Shakira danced to it on Jimmy Fallon and, despite the Chicken Shop Date redux happening four years ago, Theroux still references it approximately once every 45 seconds on his podcast.

There is also the tidal wave of interest generated by her romance (showmance? Fauxmance?) with Andrew Garfield, with whom she had shared some conspicuous chemistry on various red carpets. When he finally appeared on Chicken Shop Date in 2024, public intrigue was so high that the episode ended up getting 13m views. What’s most fascinating about this is how quickly the chemistry turned to ash as soon as the cameras started rolling. The pair looked stilted and awkward, as if they’d just realised the world expected them to be its performing monkeys. It was one of the show’s biggest moments, but also a timely reminder that not all dates are dead certs.

Other, smaller moments are just as indelible. In 2022, Matty Healy treated his appearance as an actual romantic opportunity, teasing Dimoldenberg, holding her hand and, right at the end, pestering her for a kiss for an uncomfortable length of time. In 2024, Billie Eilish played the same trick, holding Dimoldenberg’s gaze for so long that the host became visibly flustered.

Of course, purists will prefer the earlier episodes, when Dimoldenberg would use the show to deliberately weird out some much more niche British musicians. An early video, before Chicken Shop Date had established its visual identity, saw Dimoldenberg pull a variety of increasingly disgusted faces at grime MC Ghetts as he discussed the physical side of his love life.

Another, slightly later one, with Raleigh Ritchie (real name Jacob Anderson) perhaps saw the moment when the show’s potential came into clearest focus. She spent the interview chiding Ritchie for his poor posture, then seemingly provoked him into unwittingly stumbling into an immediately retracted Jimmy Savile impersonation.

It’s this essence, far more than the format or the guests, that have propelled Amelia Dimoldenberg to fame. As long as she can maintain what made her so special – the flirtiness, the awkwardness, the sense that she changed her mind about being wherever she is as soon as she got there – then she’s bound to have a long career ahead of her. If not, well … we’ll always have the chicken.

Tall tales: the 20 best giants in film – ranked!

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 12:00:28 GMT

On the 300th anniversary of Gulliver’s Travels, we celebrate the biggest film stars of them all – from a stone colossus to a metal-munching alien and a 50ft woman on the rampage

Not a first-person-shooter BFG, alas, but one of Steven Spielberg’s worst films, reducing Roald Dahl’s story to digital pap. Mo-cap Mark Rylance, whose cutesy ungrammatical babbling should have been left on the printed page, is the 24ft Big Friendly Giant who kidnaps an orphan girl, Sophie. Ugh. Big Creepy Giant, more like.

Nicholas Hoult plays the farmhand who forms an implausible alliance with a princess in a fairytale cluttered with extraneous characters. Bill Nighy plays half of a two-headed giant, but the actors are swamped by digital effects and anti-giant propaganda. The best bit is when a massive chef rolls an extraneous Ewan McGregor in pastry and puts him in an oven.

“Stone giants!” JRR Tolkien seemingly preferred dwarves to the big people, but Peter Jackson’s three-part rendering of his stand-alone children’s classic is briefly enlivened by stone colossuses hurling boulders at each other in a thunderstorm. Though one can’t help thinking how awesome a Ray Harryhausen version might have been.

Robbie Coltrane, at his least Cracker-esque, embodies lovable half-giant Rubeus Hagrid, Hogwarts groundskeeper, throughout the Potter saga, but in the standout fourth instalment we also meet Madame Maxime (Frances de la Tour), a gigantic headmistress whose academy is competing in the Triwizard Tournament. A giant love awaits.

An army colonel is accidentally exposed to a plutonium blast in Bert I Gordon’s low-budget B-movie. Instead of killing him, the radiation makes him grow to over 60ft tall. Unfortunately, it also drives him insane, and he stomps all over Las Vegas like a colicky baby in a makeshift nappy.

The Jack Black version from 2010 is barely watchable, so try this Max Fleischer production from the animation studio that brought you Popeye. Gulliver is washed up on the shores of Lilliput, where he looms large over the tiny inhabitants. On the downside, it’s a musical, and you will never be able to scrub It’s a Hap-Hap-Happy Day from your brain.

Best avoided by anyone allergic to rubbish special effects, this B-movie lives up to its iconic poster only in its final 10 minutes – but it’s such an infuriating account of an unfaithful husband gaslighting his wife that you look forward to her wreaking vengeance. Sure enough, alien radiation triggers a growth spurt and she goes on the rampage in a makeshift bikini.

Kirk Douglas plays the wily voyager in a Dino De Laurentiis/Carlo Ponti production, co-starring a stunning Silvana Mangano as both Circe and Penelope. Uncredited Mario Bava directed the scenes with the Cyclops (Italian wrestler Umberto Silvestri) during which Ulysses and his crew steal not just the giant’s sheep but also his cheese. Can you blame him for trying to eat the home invaders? Justice for Polyphemus!

André Øvredal made his solo directing debut with a found-footage account of students stumbling across a government conspiracy to conceal the existence of Norway’s national folk monster. Taking a cue from Theodor Kittelsen’s paintings, a wide range of trolls are depicted, the biggest being the 50-metre-tall Jötunn – an Old Norse word for giant.

Albert Finney tells his son porky pies about a colourful past full of witches and freaks, including a giant called Karl – a dignified performance by Matthew McGrory, who was 2.29 metres (7ft 6in) tall and holder of the Guinness World Record for longest toe. In my case, 100 minutes of yelling at Tim Burton’s exasperating whimsy are followed by a last half-hour of blubbing as the tall stories are revealed as true, sort of.

Susan, voiced by Reese Witherspoon, is rejected by her fiance after she is hit by a meteorite and grows to gargantuan size. But when Earth is threatened by aliens, it’s up to her and fellow freaks (including an insect-headed boffin) to save the planet, in a lovely animated homage to 1950s sci-fi.

“You wouldn’t like me when I’m angry.” Before Mark Ruffalo, the angst-ridden green giant was played by Eric Bana in Ang Lee’s live-action Greek tragedy wrapped in comic-book clothes. Marvel fans never fully embraced it, but is there another film in which Hulk hurls tanks around? Or fights a mutant killer poodle? I rest my case.

Gort from The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951) is the obvious choice for your outstanding giant robot, but I’m picking the metal-munching alien in Brad Bird’s directorial debut, an animated anti-war fable set in 1950s Maine during the cold war. That gravelly robo-voice belongs to Vin Diesel! And, yes, this is probably the only film where he makes you cry.

Idris Elba plays a pointy-eared djinn in George Miller’s daft but captivating romantic folly. Tilda Swinton polishes a bottle she buys in Istanbul and shazam! The tale-spinning, wish-granting djinn’s size varies from roof-raisingly gigantic to just very, very tall. His lower half is kingfisher blue and oddly indistinct, but he is probably the only giant in these rankings you, or indeed Tilda, might wish to get intimate with.

Casanova (Donald Sutherland) is about to drown himself in a Cinecittà version of the Thames when he is distracted by a female giant, played by Sandra Elaine Allen (2.31 metres, or 7ft 7in). He follows her to a fair, where they arm wrestle, one of the many surreal episodes in Fellini’s exquisite, melancholy adaptation of the 18th-century libertine’s memoirs. Nino Rota contributes one of his most haunting scores.

One of the most thrilling set-pieces in Christopher Nolan’s epic Homer adaptation is when Odysseus and his men are trapped in a cave by the 60ft Cyclops, played by Bill Irwin with a combination of animatronics, puppetry, on-set performance and a single sideways eye. Justice (at last) for Polyphemus!

Sir Gawain (Dev Patel) has encounters both earthly and supernatural as he rides to meet the Green Knight’s challenge in David Lowery’s fantasy epic. He and a fox watch from a hill as ethereal giants drift through the landscape. Are the otherworldly entities real, or a consequence of swallowing some dubious berries?

A posse of directors, including Michael Powell, bring Alexander Korda’s Arabian Nights fantasy to the screen. The special effects still look impressive, especially the towering genie (Rex Ingram in a red loincloth) who tries to crush child actor Sabu beneath his enormous foot. Check out those huge toenails!

French wrestler André the Giant (2.24 metres, or 7ft 4in) said his favourite thing about taking part in Rob Reiner’s postmodern fairytale was: “Nobody looks at me.” In other words, as Fezzik the rhymester, he was treated like an actor. He duly delivers cinema’s most moving and authentic performance by a real-life giant, no special effects necessary.

Ray Harryhausen’s stop-motion bronze statue turning its head is one of the most awe-inspiring moments in film history, the acme of cinema giants, supplemented as it is by an epic Bernard Herrmann score. Knuckleheaded Hercules steals from the treasure chamber of the gods, so Talos creaks into life and flips the Argo upside down. Hard not to feel sorry for the big lug when Jason drains it of life-giving ichor; it was only doing its job. Justice for Talos!

Women are giving their partners the ‘Illiterate Boyfriend’ test: ‘Do your best to pronounce these words’

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 11:00:51 GMT

People online are distressed at men butchering words such as ‘hyperbole’ and ‘hors d’oeuvres’ – highlighting a gender reversal in ‘intelligence gaps’

There are common non-negotiables we look for in a prospective partner. They should be kind, caring and thoughtful. Having a shared interest helps. So does remembering important dates and anniversaries. But how much does it matter if they know how to pronounce the word “gnocchi”?

Turns out that’s a potential dealbreaker, at least according to a (rather judgy) cohort on TikTok. See: the “Illiterate Boyfriend” trend, which is testing some couples on the app. Users have compiled a list of what are essentially SAT words for women to ask their male partners to read. Many of these men – this is an overwhelmingly heterosexual activity – fail to finish the list unscathed. They trip over entries such as “hyperbole”, “cynicism”, “diaphragmatic” and the oft-butchered French term, “hors d’oeuvres”.

“I want you to do your best to pronounce these words,” one woman asks her boyfriend in a clip viewed more than 8.8m times. He gamely nails his first attempt, reading off the herb “thyme”. But he’s less successful with “epitome”, “challah” and “fuchsia”. (“Foo-chia?” he guesses). “Conscientious” and “faux pas” also prove tricky. He ends up with a score of five out of 17, or 29% – very much a failing grade.

The couple laughed through the exercise, but viewers were not as charmed by an adult man struggling through what they considered basic vocabulary. “The fact that his vote matters just as much as mine is really pissing me off,” one woman wrote in the comments section. “I’m gonna be honest girl, this is worth breaking up with him over,” read another comment.

Two of the words the man correctly identified were “colonel” and “regime”, which, to one user, was evidence of a red flag: “he’s obviously a Republican”. (Maybe he just has an interest in military history, a time-honored hobby of boyfriends everywhere.) Regardless of political affiliation, it seemed fair game to dunk on Mr Foo-chia. One final quip from a viewer: “He’d be so upset if he could read these comments.”

The test made its way around TikTok, with more young couples joining in, to similarly bleak results. Even those men who did well got caught up in the pop-misandry circus. One man zipped through the list, ending with a perfect score and a self-satisfied grin. It was not the flex he might have hoped for. “This is the barest fckn minimumest [sic] of bare minimums,” one woman commented. “The men are being praised for literacy we’re in hell,” wrote another.

Distress over so-called “intelligence gaps” brings to mind a phenomenon that reverses decades of dating precedent: women are now more likely to marry less-educated men than men are to marry less-educated women. This is not necessarily by women’s choice; it is the new dating pool. According to a 2024 Pew Research report, in 1995, young men and women were equally likely to hold a bachelor’s degree. Now, 47% of women ages 25 to 34 have one, compared with 37% of their male counterparts.

“We do have in our mating market an oversupply of educated women and an undersupply of formally educated men – I’m talking academically, not necessarily in their skill set, emotional or social intelligence,” said Dr Wendy Walsh, a clinical psychologist and expert at DatingNews. com.

Dr Jess Carbino is a former sociologist for Tinder and Bumble who studies dating apps. When she polls people on what they look for in a partner, “intelligence” is rarely in the top three desired traits. “They say things like humor, kindness, attractiveness, typically,” she said. “Maybe people on the coasts – New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco – might say intelligence. But by and large, that’s not one of the top things being measured.” And there are so many different ways to consider intelligence, spelling being a way to formally test fourth-graders, not romantic partners.

One thing people do want is an equal. “It’s not necessarily that someone needs a specific degree or to know every word in the dictionary,” said Robin Hamilton, a couples therapist. “It’s more: are you able to communicate with me, are you able to meet me halfway with the subjects that I’m talking about?”

One of those subjects might be reading, an indicator of vocabulary range. Men’s rates of book reading have slipped over the past decade; nearly half of all women read just one novel or short story in 2022, but only one in four men did. According to data from Tinder, mentions of books in bios on the dating app jumped 40% this year among women, but only 23% among men. Women believe they see this disparity playing out on TikTok, even if it is through an ultimately meaningless list.

It is elitist – and naive – to draw any real conclusions about what makes a good partner based on a reading test. This “Illiterate Boyfriend” list contains words that may be more indicator of class than intelligence, conflating education with one trait women have prioritized for hundreds of years, mostly due to necessity: having money.

But the trend also reflects a wider disillusionment among straight women, who are significantly less likely to want to date than men are, partly because they say it’s hard to find someone who checks all their boxes. “He looks at the word ‘queue’ and pronounces it ‘qwi-wee’?” one woman said in a video responding to the test. “And you still have sex with him?”

“It’s rage bait for women who are frustrated and angry with the mating marketplace that is slanted unfairly” against women, Walsh said, adding: “It’s OK to date a guy who can’t say epitome or niçoise. I have a PhD, but I need spellcheck for hors d’oeuvres.”

Ben-Gvir posts Palestinians on conveyor belts to detention camps. The world is silent

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 10:00:51 GMT

Ben-Gvir did not come into power in a vacuum: he was helped into his position by an international community that has afforded Israel complete impunity

Let me introduce you to Itamar Ben-Gvir, the leader of Israel’s far-right Jewish Power (Otzma Yehudit) party, the minister of national security, and an almost cartoonishly evil man. You’ll have heard his name before: he made international news when he filmed himself taunting bound activists who had been detained trying to deliver humanitarian aid to Gaza. But you might not be familiar with many of his recent shocking comments, because they haven’t been widely covered by much of the US media.

Let’s start with an AI-generated video that Ben-Gvir posted on Twitter/X on Sunday and then deleted. It shows portly Palestinian prisoners being loaded on to a conveyor belt and going into a detention camp, then emerging emaciated. The caption is “we promised – we delivered!” which seems to be a reference to the national security minister’s promise to worsen conditions for Palestinian prisoners. An ambitious goal, considering conditions are already hellish: Israeli human rights group B’Tselem has likened the prisons where Palestinians are kept to “torture camps”.

I’m being diplomatic with my summary of this latest video, by the way. I suggest you go watch it yourself to fully take in how awful it is. (It may have been deleted, but it lives on online). If the podcaster Hasan Piker had tweeted something similar, with Israelis as the subject rather than Palestinians, it would be front-page news. US lawmakers, all of whom seem to be obsessed with Piker, would be demanding that the podcaster be punished.

Ben-Gvir, by the way, has some imaginative ideas for punishment. One of his sick fantasies is to put crocodiles in moats around prisons where Palestinians are held to stop prison breaks. The plan is now on hold because Israeli rights groups have said it is cruel to crocodiles.

I can’t stress enough that, in any discussion of Palestinian “prisoners”, it’s important to remember that many of these people have not gone through any sort of due process. Thousands of prisoners, including about 200 children, are held under “administrative detention”: a technocratic name for a dystopian practice.

To quote the B’Tselem definition: “In administrative detention, a person is held without trial without having committed an offense, on the grounds that he or she plans to break the law in the future. As this measure is supposed to be preventive, it has no time limit. The person is detained without legal proceedings, by order of the regional military commander, based on classified evidence that is not revealed to them.”

In other words: if you are Palestinian, heavily armed Israeli soldiers can come into your house in the middle of the night, drag you into a de facto torture chamber despite the fact that you haven’t committed a crime, and hold you there indefinitely without telling you why you’re being held or informing your family where you are.

When you hear the word “prisoner”, people like Ben-Gvir want you to think of dangerous terrorists who deserve everything they get. In reality, many are people like Layan Nasir: a 23-year-old woman who was taken away at gunpoint from her parents’ home for no clear reason and only made international news because she is a Christian.

But back to Ben-Gvir, who presides over prisoners. One of the minister of national security’s greatest achievements is a racist death penalty law that, because of the way it is worded, exclusively applies to Palestinians. Last month Ben-Gvir posted a video of a gallows complex where Palestinians convicted of terror offences will be hanged. For his birthday in June, he celebrated with a noose-themed cake.

Ben-Gvir doesn’t just want to hang his enemies; he wants more bloodshed in Gaza – which is still very much a killing field despite a so-called ceasefire. “I think we should be doing 30 to 40 targeted assassinations [in Gaza] per night,” Ben-Gvir recently said on a podcast. “Not just those who pose an immediate threat. There are people there who don’t deserve to live … They are not even people.”

I could go on and on: Ben-Gvir is a busy man. He recently filmed himself entering prison cells containing Palestinian women and taunting them. On the same podcast where he urged nightly killings in Gaza, he went on to say that he thought Israel should occupy the entirety of Gaza. And, on Monday, he stormed the al-Aqsa mosque compound in East Jerusalem, accompanied by extremist settlers and with the protection of the Israeli military.

This is something he does regularly: it is a blatant provocation and a contravention of an agreement that gives Muslims exclusive rights to worship at al-Aqsa while Jews pray at the Western Wall.

Ben-Gvir and others like him, however, want to change the decades-old status quo and have Israel control everything. “We are in charge here in Jerusalem and all of the land of Israel,” Ben-Gvir said during a 2023 visit to the compound.

Ben-Gvir is so shameless that there is no way to spin his conduct. He has been condemned and sanctioned by politicians and governments around the world. Nevertheless, Israel’s apologists have tried to cast him as a fringe figure. “Ben-Gvir’s statements do not reflect the policy of the State of Israel and should be condemned by all who care about Israel’s future,” the American Jewish Committee stated in August, after the politician’s comments about settlement in Gaza.

Some of Ben-Gvir’s peers have also tried to distance themselves from the extremist. The foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, condemned the video where Ben-Gvir taunts foreign activists saying: “You are not the face of Israel.”

Make no mistake: Ben-Gvir may be an embarrassment, but he is no anomaly. He is very much the face of modern Israel and his vision for the country accurately reflects the reality on the ground.

“Israeli policy is directed toward making life unbearable for Palestinians wherever they live, so that their emigration can be described as an act of free will,” the Israeli journalist Amira Hass wrote in Haaretz this week. “‘Erasure’ is the nightmare solution being written into reality every day.” Settler violence is escalating, more land in the West Bank and Gaza is being seized, and there has been widespread dehumanization of Palestinians in Israeli society.

Hass writes: “Together, these and similar forces are creating the material, ideological and psychological infrastructure within Israeli-Jewish society for another mass expulsion of Palestinians and for what might accompany it: mass slaughter.”

I’m quoting Hass because she is a brilliant journalist. But, I’ll be honest, I’m also quoting her because I’m part-Palestinian and she’s Israeli. I’m quoting Hass because, by virtue of being Israeli, she is seen as someone worth listening to. The world has made it very clear that it doesn’t want to listen to Palestinians, that we are barbarians who should not be believed.

And it is this sort of widespread dehumanization that has resulted in the complete shamelessness of a man like Ben-Gvir. He did not come into power in a vacuum: he was helped into his position by an international community which has afforded Israel complete impunity. He has been aided and abetted by international media organizations that have helped demonize Palestinians, cast doubt on our claims, and manufacture consent for erasure and expulsion.

He has been bolstered by lawmakers who tell us that we must defend Israel at all costs. And now, in the wasteland that is Gaza, in the nightly pogroms by Israeli settlers in the West Bank, and in Ben-Gvir’s brazen bloodlust, we are seeing the inevitable outcome of this unconditional support. Ben-Gvir is no aberration; he is the international community’s creation.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian US columnist

The wars in Ukraine and Iran are becoming dangerously enmeshed

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 10:00:50 GMT

As the Trump administration refuses to end its war in Iran, it is steering into the storm, not out of it

Russia hasn’t yet killed large numbers of Europeans outside Ukraine, but it’s getting closer. The night of 4-5 August, an airport bus driver discovered an armed drone lying near the tarmac of the Leipzig-Halle airport, which is a central hub of Europe’s logistical support to Ukraine’s war effort. A cargo jet, meanwhile, may have struck a second drone shortly after takeoff, forcing an abrupt landing, and investigators found a third drone laden with military explosives nearby.

In 2024, incendiary devices hidden in parcels ignited in DHL cargo at the same airport. Had these detonated in the air, a major air catastrophe and large-scale civilian casualties would have ensued, probably resulting in a broader war.

The most recent incident may be what prompted the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, to get on a plane for Moscow last week. There, according to reports, he warned his counterparts against attacks on Nato territory, urged them to curb support for Iran, argued that escalation in Ukraine would backfire, and pressed for a deal with Ukraine to end the war.

Ratcliffe’s trip is unlikely to have much impact on the Kremlin’s plans for an escalation against Ukraine in the coming months – but it is further evidence of the dangerous and growing enmeshment of the Iran and Ukraine wars.

Sending Ratcliffe to Moscow is a logical choice for the White House, given the substantial role the intelligence services play in Putin’s government and justifiable concern that he may be getting too-rosy assessments of the war from his own team. The attempt at diplomacy is to be applauded. Nevertheless, the Trump administration’s refusal to end the war with Iran is working at cross purposes with their effort to end the war in Ukraine. They are steering into the storm, not out of it.

One of the reasons for Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow, according to the Washington Post, was to dispel the Kremlin’s belief that the Trump White House was distracted from Ukraine by Iran. Good luck with that. The reporting on the severe depletion of US interceptor stocks from the war on Iran is so extensive it can only have encouraged Vladimir Putin to launch even more deadly missile strikes against Ukraine’s defenseless population.

Ukraine, for its part, has sent 228 specialists and truckloads of drones to assist the Gulf states in their defense against Iranian missile strikes, prompting at least one Iranian lawmaker to declare Ukraine fair game for its own attacks. And Ukraine struck an Iranian commercial vessel in late July. Russia has meanwhile provided Iran with battlefield intelligence that make its strikes more deadly. Moscow has, of course, also long benefited from Iranian-designed drones to attack Ukraine.

Both conflicts are getting worse and going nowhere at the same time. True, Putin is in a pinch, with an economy badly damaged by Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs, but the pinch will just as easily prompt Russia’s leader toward escalation as it will restraint – especially if he sees the US distracted again in the Middle East and believes he has a window of opportunity to deal a crushing death blow to Kyiv.

Putin, like Zelensky, like Trump, and like the Iranian leadership, faces the same sunk-cost dilemma that has led so many of history’s wartime leaders to double down on fruitless military operations – from Alcibiades in Sicily, to Napoleon in Russia, to LBJ in Vietnam. If today’s leaders follow suit, the costs and escalation risks will mount while the conflicts fuse further.

Meanwhile, Xi Jinping and Putin met on Monday and will join Iran’s leaders in Bishkek this week for the annual summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. They will discuss their plan to link their energy markets even more closely and probably condemn the new “economic offensive” that the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, announced last week to intensify pressure on Iran. Beijing may not want to see either war continue, but it also does not want to see Russia or Iran lose outright, and it is still in a strong position to avoid this outcome by helping the Iranians and Russians stave off the worst effects of the war on their economies and populations.

Ratcliffe’s trip was necessary, especially in light of Russia’s reckless grey-zone operations in Europe. But it will not be enough. His predecessor, Bill Burns, once went to Moscow in an effort to warn Russia against attacking Ukraine. That intervention fell on deaf ears, as Ratcliffe’s also will.

Clearer plans to end both wars through more positive inducements are badly needed.

To start, Washington should settle with Iran by unfreezing assets and offering sanctions relief in exchange for a real ceasefire and a framework arrangement for joint control of the strait by the littoral powers. It can then work to mitigate the consequences of this loss with a major push to diversify energy supplies – through alternative routes out of the region, alternative sources such as Venezuela, and a push on renewables. Ukraine, meanwhile, needs to become more serious about neutrality. It also needs a real debate about whether hanging on to the remainder of the Donbass it controls is worth indefinitely perpetuating the war.

In the conclusion to his recent book, The Coming Storm, which traces the parallels between today’s world and the world on the eve of the first world war, the historian Odd Arne Westad writes: “A key lesson of the world before 1914 is that regional conflicts, long left unresolved, can be the powder kegs that set off a global conflagration.” As the Iran and Ukraine conflicts intertwine without an end in sight, the world’s leaders should take such warnings far more seriously. But without real pressure from their citizens, they may not.

History is not doomed to repeat itself. But you don’t need to be a renowned historian to recognize the dangers the world is throwing up before us, nor to lament the failure of our leaders to calm these storms.

Christopher S Chivvis is a senior fellow and director of the American Statecraft Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. He served as the United States national intelligence officer for Europe from 2018 to 2021

Queens of the Stone Age’s Josh Homme kicked a woman and his ex-wife alleged domestic abuse. Why the cosy makeover?

The Guardian Thu, 03 Sep 2026 09:00:48 GMT

Like Johnny Depp and Chris Brown before him, Homme has got past his chequered history to retain an adoring fanbase. Almost a decade post-#MeToo, audiences no longer seem to care

As part of the promo for Queens of the Stone Age’s new album Perfecth, the band has set up a novelty complaints hotline for fans to call. “No bitching too big, no whiny too tiny,” it promises. I’ll bite: how about the fact that frontman Josh Homme’s ex-wife Brody Dalle testified in court that he head-butted her so hard that she “saw stars” and said he had fantasised about killing her? Or that he kicked a female photographer in the face? It’s certainly not what anyone’s talking about as part of Homme’s friendly neighbourhood rock star image rehabilitation: duetting on Shania Twain’s new album, taking the couch on Celebrity Gogglebox, teatime BBC 6 Music interviews.

Homme and Dalle clearly had a complicated relationship: he allegedly tried to throw her boyfriend off a balcony; he claims that she was violent towards him; both have taken out restraining orders against one another; Homme has full custody of their kids after Dalle’s boyfriend was found to have forged her signature on an application for a restraining order. Homme has recently talked about coming through a dark period, including successful treatment for cancer, and getting a handle on his vices. Nevertheless, there is clear footage of him brutally kicking the camera of photographer Chelsea Lauren back into her face, which he acknowledged in an apology video, and court testimony from Dalle alleging that a drunk Homme told her “I want to fucking strangle you right now” on one occasion, and head-butted her on another.

Their situation shares resonances with Johnny Depp and Amber Heard’s messy relationship breakdown, which prompted a British judge to deem that the Sun was in fact accurate in labelling Depp a “wife-beater” despite his libel claim against them; although a US jury ruled in his favour against Heard, who was found guilty of defamation. You only have to see the grim trailer for Ebenezer, Depp’s forthcoming Scrooge trauma plot movie, to see how much any of this really damaged his career. “It’s good to be back,” Depp-as-Scrooge tee-hees in his first spoken scene. Subtext, as Garth Marenghi told us, is for cowards. Text appears proclaiming “the master of misfits returns”; the entire aesthetic seems skimmed from former Depp hits Sweeney Todd, Pirates of the Caribbean and Edward Scissorhands. As someone says in the comments: “This entire trailer is just, ‘You like Johnny Depp right?’” You could sum up most of the rest of the comments as: we sure do! Nothing says future Christmas classic like big-budget reputation laundering.

You get the hopeless feeling that none of this matters any more. Chris Brown is currently on a high-profile US tour with Usher that has had guest appearances from trailblazing female artists such as Alicia Keys and Mary J Blige – despite him beating then-girlfriend Rihanna in 2009 and another ex being granted a five-year restraining order after he threatened her. “For years, traditional media has been tiptoeing around the popularity of Chris Brown, and in reality, that benefits nobody but him,” critic Alphonse Pierre wrote in a pan of Brown’s latest album, Brown. “The lack of critical engagement with his music has allowed him to contextualise his own redemption with statistic and sob stories.” And yet, as Doreen St Felix wrote in the New Yorker, the tour’s audience is full of adoring women.

Almost a decade after the mainstream #MeToo movement, it’s clear that audiences’ nostalgia for artists who made art that meant something to them at a formative age overrides the inconvenience of violence against women. Couple that fondness with an expensive publicity campaign and the counternarrative never stands a chance, easily dismissed as the shrill cries of cranks. I believe firmly in rehabilitation and second chances, but haven’t been able to shake a sense of horror that millions of people can apparently look past allegations and evidence of violence against women when engaging in supposedly feelgood pop culture.

Last month, Homme made headlines during a Detroit show where he flouted the venue’s smoking ban, risking a $10,000 fine to take a stand against “fuckin’ corporate assholes” who “tell you what to do” (while his band, um, voluntarily play those corporate assholes’ corporate venue for a fat pay cheque). This sort of limp rock’n’roll cosplay is just as cosy in its own way as reviewing crap British TV on primetime Channel 4: vanilla rebellion figures offering the comforting reassurance that rock stars still walk among us, boldly reminding us that rules are made to be broken.

The notion of so-called rock’n’roll behaviour, many have theorised, was partly why music never had much of a “#MeToo moment”, that hopeless relic of a phrase. When bad behaviour isn’t just accepted but venerated, real wrongdoing can be brushed under the same whisky-stained rug. Blind eyes are turned, offenders are remade as outlaws, myths are upheld, party lines toed: “It’s so safe to play along / Little soldiers in a row,” as Homme sang in Go With the Flow. The jokey complaints hotline might be the most honest part of QOTSA’s return: a grim reflection of the fact that nobody is taking this shit seriously any more.
